domains.name: Information Literacy & Source Evaluation
domains.summary: Covers how scholarly knowledge is produced and published, how learners turn an assignment topic into a searchable question, how they search catalogues and databases, and how they judge whether a source is trustworthy and fit for a specific purpose. Evaluation is treated as contextual judgement, in line with the ACRL frame 'Authority Is Constructed and Contextual', rather than as checklist compliance, and lateral reading is included as an empirically grounded alternative to judging a site on its own terms. The language demands are real: generating search terms draws on vocabulary depth and disciplinary terminology, and judging a source depends on reading its genre signals and paratext.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how academic knowledge is published, how to find relevant sources efficiently with library tools, and how to decide whether a source is reliable enough for the job you want it to do in your work.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Distinguishing scholarly from popular sources, simple catalogue and discovery-tool searches, and basic credibility checks, including lateral reading of web sources.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Subject databases, citation chaining from key readings, and module-specific judgements about what counts as an acceptable source.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Efficient, documented searching for dissertations, checking venues and retractions, and legitimate access to paywalled work.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Systematic or scoping searching, comprehensive citation chaining and reproducible search records maintained across a multi-year project.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Focusing a topic for a project, building keyword searches with synonyms and Boolean operators, evaluating sources for an extended essay, and keeping records that make accurate citation possible.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Focusing a topic for a project, building keyword searches with synonyms and Boolean operators, evaluating sources for an extended essay, and keeping records that make accurate citation possible.

domains.name: Summarising, Paraphrasing & Quoting
domains.summary: Covers the core textual practices by which writers bring others' words and ideas into their own texts: quoting, paraphrasing and summarising, the reporting language that attributes and evaluates source content, and the signalling that keeps the writer's voice distinct from the sources'. The domain follows research suggesting that source-use problems in L2 writing are often developmental, linked to comprehension, vocabulary and an incomplete sense of why sources are used, rather than to intent to deceive (Howard; Pecorari; Shi; Keck). Instruction therefore pairs language work with purpose: learners transform sources in order to serve their own argument, and close dependence on source wording is treated as something to be taught through, not only policed.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to quote, paraphrase and summarise sources accurately, how to make clear which ideas come from a source and which are your own, and how to choose language that reports other writers' ideas precisely.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Accurate quotation, basic signal phrases, summarising paragraphs and early paraphrasing, with close dependence on source wording treated as a normal stage to work through.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Disciplinary norms for quotation and citation form, summarising whole texts, and source use that serves analysis rather than display.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid, accurate summarising of research articles, evaluative reporting, and clear voice boundaries in dense, multi-source writing.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Fine control of reporting verbs, citation form and attribution in research writing, and transparent use of sources in other languages.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Paraphrase and summary in assessed writing, reporting verbs, voice boundaries and integration of sources in extended essays.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Paraphrase and summary in assessed writing, reporting verbs, voice boundaries and integration of sources in extended essays.

domains.name: Synthesis
domains.summary: Covers discourse synthesis: building a new text that integrates several sources around the writer's own organising ideas rather than summarising them one by one. The domain moves from the concept of synthesis, through tools for organising sources (matrices and thematic grouping), to the language of relating sources, identifying gaps and tensions, and writing synthesis paragraphs, and includes integrated reading- and listening-to-writing tasks. Spivey's account of synthesis as organising, selecting and connecting, together with research on integrated writing (Plakans; Plakans and Gebril; Grabe and Zhang), frames synthesis as a constructive reading–writing process rather than a set of linking phrases.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to bring several sources together around your own ideas, show how they agree, differ and leave questions open, and complete tasks that combine reading, listening and writing.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Understanding synthesis versus serial summary, simple matrices built from two or three sources, and short integrated tasks.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Synthesising module readings in essays and literature review assignments, with explicit relationships between sources and, in final-year projects, identification of gaps.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Literature reviews that group sources by theme, relate them critically and identify gaps that justify a dissertation question.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Synthesising large, contested literatures and articulating tensions and gaps that position an original contribution.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Thematic grouping and synthesis paragraphs in extended essays, and integrated reading-into-writing tasks used for progression decisions.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Thematic grouping and synthesis paragraphs in extended essays, and integrated reading-into-writing tasks used for progression decisions.

topics.name: Types of sources
topics.description: Classify sources by their relation to the object of study (primary, secondary, tertiary), by the kind of knowledge they offer (empirical study, review, theoretical or conceptual work, practice or policy document) and by their intended readership (scholarly or popular). Classification tells the learner what a source can legitimately support, and it depends on the discipline and question: a newspaper report is a secondary source for a chemist but may be a primary source for a historian.
masteryEvidence: Classifies a mixed set of sources as primary, secondary or tertiary for a stated discipline and justifies borderline cases
Distinguishes an empirical research article from a review article and a theoretical paper using the abstract, headings and reference list
Identifies whether a text is written for specialists or the general public from its venue, paratext and language
Explains what each source type can and cannot support in an assignment, for example using an encyclopaedia for orientation but not as evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner six records with first pages (a journal research article, a review, a textbook chapter, a news report, a government report and a blog post). Ask them to classify each and state one thing it could support in an essay on a given question. Check whether they use evidence from the text rather than format or location alone, and whether they recognise that 'primary' depends on the discipline.

topics.name: How scholarly knowledge is produced
topics.description: Explain how academic knowledge is made public and checked: peer review, journal articles, monographs and edited books, conference papers, preprints and grey literature, and the versions a single study may pass through. This understanding underpins calibrated judgements about authority, currency and status, for example why a preprint is cited with caution and why a textbook lags behind the journal literature.
masteryEvidence: Describes the main stages of peer review and states what it does and does not guarantee
Distinguishes a preprint, an accepted manuscript and a version of record of the same article and states which to cite
Explains why conference papers carry high status in some fields, such as computing, and lower status in others
Identifies grey literature (reports, theses, policy papers) and gives a reason it may be valuable despite not being peer reviewed
Relates the time a format takes to produce to how current its content is likely to be
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner the same study as a preprint-server record and as a published journal article. Ask what may have changed between the two, which they would cite and why. Check whether they mention peer review and possible changes to findings, and whether they avoid assuming that 'published' means 'true'.

topics.name: Focusing a topic for searching
topics.description: Narrow a broad assignment topic into a focused question by specifying context, population, period, variables or perspective, and test whether it is answerable within the word limit and the available literature. A focused question yields usable search concepts and inclusion decisions; an unfocused one produces unmanageable or irrelevant results and descriptive writing.
masteryEvidence: Reformulates a broad topic as a question that names its key concepts and at least two limiting dimensions, such as context and population
Identifies the concepts in the question that will become separate search blocks
Adjusts the scope of the question after a trial search returns too many or too few relevant results
Checks that the focused question still answers the assignment task and its command words
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a broad essay title (for example on social media and wellbeing) and a 2,000-word limit. Ask for a focused question and the key concepts they would search for. Check that the question is answerable, limited in at least two dimensions, still meets the brief, and yields distinct search concepts.

topics.name: Search strategies
topics.description: Build and refine searches by breaking a question into concepts, generating synonyms, spelling variants and broader or narrower terms for each, and combining them with Boolean operators, truncation, phrase searching and filters. Searching is iterative: learners read early results to harvest better terms and revise the strategy rather than typing a whole question into a search box.
masteryEvidence: Produces a concept table with synonyms, British and American spellings, and broader and narrower terms for each concept
Combines terms with OR within a concept and AND between concepts, using brackets correctly
Uses truncation and phrase searching appropriately and recognises when truncation retrieves unwanted words
Refines a search with terms harvested from the titles, abstracts and subject headings of relevant results
Applies filters (date, language, document type, peer review) and justifies each choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a focused question and ask for one database search string. Check for concept blocks, synonyms joined with OR, blocks joined with AND, correct bracketing and sensible truncation, and ask what they would change if the search returned 3,000 results.

topics.name: Library catalogues, databases and discovery tools
topics.description: Choose between the library catalogue, the discovery layer, subject databases and Google Scholar according to what each indexes and how it can be searched, and use each tool's features (subject headings, filters, export, citation links, full-text links). Knowing what a tool covers stops learners concluding that 'there is nothing on this topic' after one search in an unsuitable tool.
masteryEvidence: Selects an appropriate tool for a stated need, such as the catalogue for a known book or a subject database for recent empirical studies
Names at least one subject database for their own field and states what it covers
Uses database-specific features such as thesaurus terms, peer-review filters and export to a reference manager
Reaches the full text of an item through library links rather than paying publishers or abandoning the item
Explains one strength and one limitation of Google Scholar compared with a subject database
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to find two peer-reviewed empirical articles from the last five years on a given question, narrating which tool they use and why. Check tool choice, use of filters, whether they reach the full text through the library, and whether they can explain why results differ between Google Scholar and the database.

topics.name: Evaluating sources
topics.description: Judge whether a source is credible and fit for a specific purpose by weighing its authority, currency, relevance, purpose and evidence base against the task. Evaluation is contextual: the same source may be acceptable as an example of public debate but inadequate as evidence for a causal claim, and checklists help only when applied with judgement.
masteryEvidence: Justifies including or excluding a source with reasons tied to the purpose it will serve in the assignment
Identifies who produced a source, their expertise and their interests, using evidence beyond the source's own claims about itself
Judges how current a source needs to be for different questions and fields
Checks whether claims in a source are supported by data, references or methods, and notes where they are not
Explains why a peer-reviewed source can still be unsuitable and a non-peer-reviewed source can still be appropriate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three sources on one question (a peer-reviewed study, a think-tank report and a well-referenced news feature) and an essay purpose. Ask which they would use, for what, and why. Check that judgements are purpose-specific, go beyond 'it is peer reviewed' or 'it is a .org site', and draw on evidence about the producer and the evidence base.

topics.name: Lateral reading
topics.description: Evaluate an unfamiliar website, organisation, author or claim by leaving it and opening new tabs to find out what independent, reliable sources say about it, rather than judging it from its appearance and 'About' page. Wineburg and McGrew found that professional fact-checkers worked this way and reached sounder judgements more quickly than historians and students who read vertically within the site.
masteryEvidence: Leaves an unfamiliar site early to search for information about its publisher, funder or author
Uses reference works, independent news coverage and searches on the organisation's name to establish its reputation and interests
Exercises click restraint by scanning a page of search results before choosing which link to open
Traces a quoted statistic or claim back to its original source before using it
Explains why professional design, a .org domain or a self-description is weak evidence of reliability
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the homepage of a plausible advocacy organisation with a neutral-sounding name and ask, with a five-minute limit, whether its report on a contested issue is a reliable source. Check whether they leave the site to investigate its funding and stance, or judge it from design, domain and self-description.

topics.name: Predatory publishing, retractions and misinformation
topics.description: Recognise the main routes by which unreliable material enters the record: deceptive ('predatory') venues that take fees without genuine peer review, published work that is later corrected or retracted, and misinformation that circulates through repeated citation, social media and fabricated references from generative AI tools. Learners need to verify venues and article status, and to understand that publication alone is not proof.
masteryEvidence: Identifies warning signs of a deceptive journal (implausibly fast review, aggressive solicitation, unverifiable indexing or metric claims) and verifies them through independent sources
Checks whether an article has been corrected, retracted or flagged with an expression of concern before citing it
Explains why a retracted article may still appear in search results and be cited by others
Traces a widely repeated claim to its origin to test whether it is supported
Locates every reference suggested by an AI tool in a library database before using it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a reference to an article in a little-known journal and an email inviting submission to a similar journal. Ask whether they would cite or submit, and what they would check first. Check whether they verify indexing and editorial claims independently, check the article's status, and avoid judging from the title or a claimed impact factor.

topics.name: Citation chaining
topics.description: Use a relevant source as a node in the scholarly conversation: follow its references backward to earlier work and use 'cited by' tools to follow later work forward. Chaining finds sources that keyword searches miss, reveals key works in a debate and shows how a claim has been taken up, extended or challenged.
masteryEvidence: Selects references to follow from a source's introduction or literature review, giving a reason based on how the citing text uses each
Locates the full text of a cited work from a reference entry in an unfamiliar referencing system
Uses a 'cited by' function to find later work and filters it for relevance
Identifies works cited across several sources as likely key texts
Notes how later work has supported, extended or challenged an earlier claim
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner one recent review article on their topic. Ask for three earlier works worth following and two later works that cite the review, with a reason for each. Check whether choices are driven by how the work is used rather than its position in the list, whether they can decode the reference format, and whether they use a citation index for forward chaining.

topics.name: Recording searches and sources
topics.description: Keep records that allow searches to be repeated and sources to be found and cited accurately: tools searched, search strings, filters, dates and result counts, together with complete bibliographic details and locators for each source used. Good records prevent lost references and inaccurate citations, and protect against unattributed borrowing when the origin of a note has been forgotten.
masteryEvidence: Records the bibliographic details needed for the source type at the point of first reading, including page numbers or other locators
Maintains a search log with tool, date, search string, filters and number of results
Uses a consistent filing system or reference manager so that any note can be traced to its source
Re-runs a logged search and obtains comparable results
topics.assessmentPrompt: Two weeks after a search task, ask the learner to retrieve the exact source behind one of their notes and to re-run the search that found it. Check whether their records (string, tool, date, filters, full reference, locator) allow this without starting again.

topics.name: Open access and legal access
topics.description: Understand the routes by which scholarly work is made freely available (open-access journals with or without author charges, self-archiving in repositories, preprints) and the legitimate ways of obtaining paywalled work (library subscriptions, interlibrary loan, author copies, legal open-access finders). This lets learners find accessible versions, cite the right version and recognise the legal and security problems of unauthorised download sites.
masteryEvidence: Explains the main open-access routes in terms of who pays and where the work is held
Locates a legal open version of a paywalled article through a repository or open-access discovery tool
Requests an item through interlibrary loan or asks an author for a copy
Identifies which version (preprint, accepted manuscript, version of record) has been found and cites accordingly
Explains why open access does not in itself indicate quality, either high or low
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a reference to a paywalled article and ten minutes to obtain a legitimate copy, reporting each step. Check whether they use library access, repositories, open-access finders or interlibrary loan rather than unauthorised sites, and whether they identify the version found.

topics.name: Systematic and scoping searching
topics.description: Design and report a transparent, reproducible search for a systematic, scoping or structured literature review: a protocol with a defined question, sources, full search strings for each database, supplementary methods such as chaining, explicit eligibility criteria and a record of screening decisions. Expectations depend on the field: such searching is standard in health and other evidence-synthesis fields and increasingly expected in education and social-policy dissertations.
masteryEvidence: Writes a search strategy that another person can run to reproduce the results, including database-specific syntax and subject headings
States explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria and applies them consistently at title, abstract and full-text screening
Documents the numbers of records identified, screened, excluded and included, following the field's reporting guideline
Justifies the choice of databases and supplementary searches for the review question
Distinguishes the aims and search expectations of systematic, scoping and narrative reviews
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to swap search strategies with a peer and run each other's strategy in the same database. Check whether the peer obtains the same results, whether criteria are explicit enough to apply without consulting the author, and whether the learner can name the reporting guideline their field expects.

topics.name: Quoting
topics.description: Decide when direct quotation is warranted (the wording itself is the object of analysis, is a definition or formulation that cannot be bettered, or carries authority in the field) and quote accurately and economically, marking omissions and insertions and giving a locator. Norms differ by discipline: quotation is routine in the humanities and much social science but rare in the natural sciences and engineering.
masteryEvidence: Justifies each quotation by the reason its exact wording matters
Reproduces quoted wording, spelling and punctuation exactly
Shortens quotations to the essential words, marking omissions with ellipses and insertions with square brackets without changing the meaning
Includes a page or other locator as the referencing style requires
Adjusts the frequency and length of quotation to the conventions of the target discipline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 200-word source passage and a paragraph that needs support from it. Ask them to add one quotation. Check whether they choose a phrase whose wording matters rather than a sentence of routine information, quote it exactly, mark any omission correctly and include a locator.

topics.name: Integrating quotations
topics.description: Embed quotations grammatically and rhetorically: introduce them with a frame that names the source and signals relevance or stance, fit quoted fragments into the syntax of the surrounding sentence, and follow them with commentary that interprets the quotation and connects it to the writer's point. Unframed, 'dropped' quotations leave the reader to infer their relevance and blur the writer's voice.
masteryEvidence: Introduces every quotation with a signal phrase or framing clause that identifies the source and its relevance
Integrates partial quotations so that the combined sentence is grammatical, adjusting the frame rather than the quoted words
Follows a quotation with at least one sentence of interpretation or evaluation linking it to the paragraph's point
Chooses between run-in, block and partial quotation according to length and the style guide
Avoids ending a paragraph on an uncommented quotation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a paragraph containing two dropped quotations and one ungrammatical partial quotation, and ask for a revision. Check for an introductory frame, grammatical integration, follow-up commentary that interprets rather than repeats, and no unmarked changes to quoted words.

topics.name: Paraphrasing
topics.description: Restate a specific idea from a source in substantially new wording and sentence structure while preserving its meaning, scope and degree of certainty, and attribute it. Paraphrase lets writers integrate sources into their own argument rather than stitching quotations together, and it depends on full comprehension of the source before reformulation begins.
masteryEvidence: Produces a paraphrase that a reader judges equivalent in meaning, including hedges, qualifications and scope
Changes both vocabulary and sentence structure without retaining strings of source wording beyond technical terms and fixed expressions
Retains discipline-specific technical terms that should not be synonymised
Attributes the paraphrase with a correctly formatted citation and signals where the attributed content ends
Judges whether a given paraphrase is acceptable, too close to its source or distorted, and explains why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 50–70-word paragraph containing one hedged claim and one technical term. Ask for a paraphrase written with the source covered. Check whether meaning and certainty are preserved, structure as well as vocabulary is changed, the technical term is kept, and a citation is included.

topics.name: Paraphrasing techniques
topics.description: Control the lexicogrammatical operations used in reformulation: substitution with near-synonyms, word-class change, voice change, nominalisation and its reverse, clause reordering and combining, and change of perspective. Learners also need the limits of each operation: synonym substitution alone yields patchwriting, near-synonyms can shift meaning or strength, and technical terms should usually be kept.
masteryEvidence: Transforms a sentence using at least three different operations (for example word-class change, voice change and clause reordering) while preserving its meaning
Selects near-synonyms that match the source's meaning, strength and collocation, and rejects those that do not
Identifies words in a source sentence that are technical terms or names and should be kept
Explains why replacing words one for one while keeping the source's structure does not produce an acceptable paraphrase
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a source sentence and four reformulations: a one-for-one synonym swap, a version with a meaning-changing near-synonym, a restructured version, and a version that replaces a technical term. Ask them to rank the versions and explain. Check whether they identify the too-close and distorted versions and justify keeping the technical term.

topics.name: Patchwriting
topics.description: Understand patchwriting (reproducing a source's structure and much of its wording with some words deleted, substituted or rearranged) as a common and contested stage in learning to write from sources, distinct from deliberate copying, and use strategies to move beyond it. Howard and Pecorari argue that it often reflects incomplete comprehension and limited linguistic resources rather than intent to deceive, although institutional policies may still classify it as plagiarism.
masteryEvidence: Identifies patchwriting by comparing a text with its source and locating retained strings and structures
Explains how patchwriting differs from paraphrase, from unmarked quotation and from deliberate plagiarism, and why its status is contested
Revises a patchwritten passage into an acceptable paraphrase or a marked quotation
Applies a comprehension-first routine (read, explain, cover, write, compare) to reduce dependence on source wording
States how their own institution's policy treats close copying with a citation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a source paragraph and a student text that patchwrites it with a citation. Ask whether it is acceptable and what they would change. Check whether they locate the retained strings and structure, recognise that a citation alone does not make borrowed wording acceptable, and revise it into a genuine paraphrase or a marked quotation.

topics.name: Summarising a passage
topics.description: Condense a paragraph or short section to its main idea and essential support, in the writer's own words and to a stated length, and attribute it to the source. Passage summary is the building block for note-making, summary–response writing and synthesis, and it depends on identifying main ideas and on reformulation.
masteryEvidence: States the main idea of a paragraph in one sentence that does not reproduce its topic sentence
Omits examples, repetition and minor detail while keeping qualifications that affect meaning
Writes the summary in own words and structure, retaining necessary technical terms
Attributes the summary to its source with a signal phrase or citation
Adjusts a summary to a specified word count without distorting the source
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 150-word paragraph and ask for a 30-word summary written without looking back. Check whether it captures the main idea, keeps any qualification that changes meaning, excludes examples, avoids copied strings and is attributed.

topics.name: Summarising a whole text
topics.description: Summarise an article or chapter by building its macrostructure: deleting trivial and redundant material, replacing lists with superordinate terms, and selecting or constructing statements that capture each section's gist (Brown and Day's macrorules). The summary represents the author's purpose, argument and main findings in proportion, using reporting language to show the author's moves.
masteryEvidence: Produces a summary that represents the text's purpose, main argument or findings and conclusion in proportion to their importance
Applies deletion, generalisation and construction rather than shortening each paragraph in turn
Uses reporting verbs that represent the author's moves (for example argues, reports, concludes)
Keeps the author's claims separate from the summariser's own views unless the task asks for evaluation
Adapts the length and focus of a summary to its purpose, such as an annotated bibliography entry or an essay's background section
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 1,500-word article and ask for a 150-word summary. Check whether it is organised around the article's macrostructure rather than its paragraph order, gives proportionate space to the main claim and findings, uses reporting verbs that fit the author's moves, and contains no unmarked evaluation.

topics.name: Reporting verbs
topics.description: Choose reporting verbs by what the source did (research acts such as find and observe; cognitive acts such as believe and assume; discourse acts such as argue, claim and note) and by the stance they convey towards the reported claim (accepting, neutral or distancing), and use their grammatical patterns accurately. Reporting verbs are a principal resource for representing sources precisely and signalling the writer's position on them.
masteryEvidence: Selects verbs that accurately describe the source's act, such as 'found' for a result and 'argued' for a position
Distinguishes verbs that commit the writer to the claim (demonstrate, show) from neutral (state, suggest) and distancing (claim, allege) ones
Uses reporting verbs with accurate complementation (that-clause, noun phrase + as, wh-clause)
Varies reporting verbs for precision rather than for variety alone
Describes the reporting-verb preferences of their own discipline from evidence in its texts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three reports of the same study using 'shows', 'suggests' and 'claims', and ask what each tells the reader about the writer's view. Then ask them to report a finding they consider weakly supported. Check whether they recognise the stance difference and choose a verb that conveys appropriate distance with correct complementation.

topics.name: Integral and non-integral citation
topics.description: Choose between integral citation, where the cited author is an element of the sentence ('Smith (2020) argues that…'), and non-integral citation, where the reference sits in brackets or a number and the information is foregrounded, according to the rhetorical effect required. Author-prominent forms highlight who said something, often to contrast positions; information-prominent forms present content as established or bundle several supporting sources. The balance between forms varies across disciplines.
masteryEvidence: Identifies integral and non-integral citations in expert texts, including integral citations where the author's name is not the grammatical subject
Explains the difference in emphasis between an author-prominent and an information-prominent version of the same citation
Uses non-integral citation to group several sources that support one point
Uses integral citation to contrast or evaluate specific scholars' positions
Relates their own balance of citation forms to the conventions of their discipline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a paragraph in which every citation is integral and sources are listed one after another. Ask them to revise it so that well-established points are information-prominent and one contested position remains author-prominent. Check whether the revision changes emphasis appropriately and whether the learner can explain why.

topics.name: Distinguishing own voice from source voice
topics.description: Make clear where source content begins and ends and where the writer's own interpretation, evaluation or argument takes over, using attribution, citation placement, averral markers and evaluative commentary. Readers need these signals to assign responsibility for claims, and markers judge both originality and integrity by them.
masteryEvidence: Marks the extent of each paraphrase or summary so that a reader can identify every attributed proposition
Signals the move from source content to own comment explicitly (for example 'This suggests…', 'However, this account overlooks…')
Places citations so that they cover the attributed content and do not appear to cover the writer's own claims
Includes the writer's own commentary in paragraphs that use sources, rather than only reporting
Identifies sentences in a peer's draft whose source status is ambiguous
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 150-word paragraph that mixes two sources with the writer's comment, with all citations at the end. Ask them to highlight what comes from each source and what is the writer's, then to revise so the boundaries are clear. Check the accuracy of the highlighting and whether the revision uses attribution and averral markers rather than simply adding more citations.

topics.name: Secondary citation
topics.description: Cite a source known only through another author's account transparently (for example with 'as cited in' in APA style), recognise when this is acceptable (the original is unobtainable or in an inaccessible language), and otherwise locate and read the original, since secondary accounts can simplify or misrepresent it. Citing an unread original as if it had been read misrepresents the writer's reading.
masteryEvidence: Formats a secondary citation correctly in the required style, including which work appears in the reference list
Attempts to locate the original before using a secondary citation
Explains why citing an unread original misrepresents the writer's reading
Limits secondary citation to cases where the original is genuinely unavailable
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a textbook sentence reporting a classic study, with its citation. Ask how they would use the claim in an essay. Check whether they try to find the original first, and if not, whether they format a secondary citation correctly and list only the work they read (in APA style).

topics.name: Using sources in other languages
topics.description: Use sources written in languages other than English transparently: translate or paraphrase their content accurately, mark one's own translations of quotations, give the original wording where conventions require, and reference the original-language work with a translated title as the style requires. Non-English scholarship can be a valuable resource, especially on local contexts, and using it well depends on clear signalling rather than silent translation.
masteryEvidence: Indicates when a quotation is the writer's own translation, following the style guide's convention
Paraphrases content from a non-English source with a citation to the original work
Formats a reference to a non-English work with its original title and, where required, a translated title
Explains why presenting translated wording without attribution is unacknowledged borrowing
Justifies including a non-English source by its relevance and checks local expectations with the tutor
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to use one point from a source in their first language in an English paragraph, once as a quotation and once as a paraphrase, with the reference-list entry. Check whether the translation is marked as theirs, the citation points to the original work, and the reference entry follows the style's rules for non-English titles.

topics.name: What synthesis is
topics.description: Understand synthesis as building a new, writer-organised account from several sources (selecting relevant content, organising it around themes or claims, and connecting sources to one another) rather than summarising sources in turn. Synthesis underlies literature reviews and source-based essays, and markers commonly distinguish it from author-by-author description.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes a synthesised paragraph from a serial summary of the same sources and explains the difference
Identifies the organising idea of a synthesis paragraph and how each source relates to it
Explains why a synthesis is organised by ideas rather than by sources
Proposes a point on which several given sources can be brought together
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner two paragraphs using the same three sources: one summarises each source in turn, the other is organised around a point. Ask which is a synthesis and why. Check whether they identify the organising idea and the connections between sources, not merely the presence of several citations.

topics.name: Synthesis matrices
topics.description: Record sources in a grid, with sources as rows and themes, aims, methods, findings or positions as columns, so that comparisons across sources become visible. The matrix is a note-making and planning tool that supports the shift from source-by-source to idea-by-idea organisation; columns can be set by the teacher or task at first and generated by the learner later.
masteryEvidence: Constructs a matrix with columns suited to the task, such as themes for an essay or design, sample and findings for empirical studies
Fills cells with concise own-words notes and locators, marking any direct quotation
Reads the matrix by column to identify agreement, disagreement and missing information across sources
Revises columns as new themes emerge from reading
Uses the matrix to plan paragraphs organised by theme
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner four short abstracts and a question. Ask them to build a matrix and then state one point on which the sources agree and one on which they differ. Check whether the columns fit the question, cells are concise and in their own words, and the points are derived from reading down columns rather than across rows.

topics.name: Grouping sources thematically
topics.description: Identify themes, issues or positions that cut across a set of sources and group the sources, or parts of them, under those themes so that a text can be organised by idea. Thematic grouping requires classifying by explicit criteria and recognising that one source may contribute to several themes.
masteryEvidence: Proposes themes that are relevant to the question and supported by more than one source
Assigns parts of sources to themes, allowing one source to appear under several themes
Names each theme with a precise phrase that could become a topic sentence or heading
Justifies the grouping criterion (by position, factor, method or finding) and considers an alternative grouping
Orders themes in a sequence that serves the argument
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner eight short source summaries on one topic and ask them to group the sources into three or four named themes. Check whether the themes are conceptually coherent and relevant to the question, whether sources appear under more than one theme where appropriate, and whether the learner can justify the grouping criterion.

topics.name: Writing relationships between sources
topics.description: Express how sources relate to one another (agreement, corroboration, extension, qualification, contrast and contradiction) using precise reporting verbs, comparison and contrast language, and citation forms that group sources or set them against each other. Making these relationships explicit is what turns a set of citations into synthesis.
masteryEvidence: Identifies whether two sources agree, whether one extends or qualifies the other, or whether they conflict
Writes sentences that state relationships explicitly (for example 'Lee (2021) extends this finding to…'; 'In contrast to earlier studies, …')
Groups agreeing sources in a single citation and sets conflicting sources against each other
Distinguishes apparent from real disagreement by checking definitions, samples and methods
Uses reporting verbs and connectors that represent each relationship accurately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two short abstracts that partly agree but differ in sample or context, and ask for two sentences relating the studies. Check whether the sentences state the relationship explicitly and precisely (for example qualification rather than simple contradiction), use accurate relational language and, where relevant, suggest the source of the difference.

topics.name: Identifying gaps and tensions
topics.description: Identify what a body of literature leaves unresolved (conflicting findings, competing interpretations, methodological limitations, under-studied populations or contexts, and untested assumptions) and express it accurately and with appropriate hedging. Gaps and tensions justify new work and give reviews and essays an argumentative direction, but a claimed gap must be grounded in the literature actually reviewed.
masteryEvidence: Identifies at least two kinds of gap or tension (for example conflicting findings, an unstudied context, a shared methodological limitation) in a set of sources
Distinguishes a genuine gap from an artefact of a limited search
Explains possible reasons for conflicting findings, such as differences in method, sample or definition
Expresses gaps with appropriate hedging and scope ('few studies have examined…' rather than 'no one has studied…')
Links an identified gap to a question that the writer's own argument or study addresses
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a synthesis matrix of six studies. Ask for two sentences identifying a gap or tension and one sentence on how a new study could address it. Check whether the gap is supported by the matrix, hedged and scoped appropriately, and specific enough to motivate a question.

topics.name: Writing synthesis paragraphs
topics.description: Write paragraphs controlled by the writer's point, in which several sources are brought into dialogue as evidence, contrast or qualification, and the writer's commentary explains what the combination shows. A synthesis paragraph typically opens with the writer's claim, uses grouped and contrasted citations, keeps voice boundaries clear, and closes by drawing out significance for the wider argument.
masteryEvidence: Opens the paragraph with a topic sentence that expresses the writer's point rather than a source's
Integrates at least three sources in relation to that point, using grouped and contrasted citations
Includes commentary that interprets the relationship between the sources
Keeps clear boundaries between each source's content and the writer's voice
Closes the paragraph by linking the synthesis to the wider argument
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a synthesis matrix with four sources and a focus question, and ask for one 150–200-word paragraph. Check that the topic sentence is the writer's claim, sources are related rather than listed, citation forms group and contrast appropriately, voice boundaries are clear, and the paragraph ends with commentary rather than a source.

topics.name: Integrated source-based tasks
topics.description: Complete tasks that require reading and/or listening to sources and producing a written (or spoken) response that selects, transforms and integrates their content, such as summary–response tasks, reading-into-writing assessments and lecture-plus-reading syntheses. Success depends on comprehension, selective note-making, transformation of source language and organisation around the task rather than around the sources.
masteryEvidence: Analyses the task to determine what must be taken from each source and how the response should be organised
Makes notes from reading and listening that capture main points and the relationships between them
Integrates content from more than one source and states how the sources relate
Transforms source language through paraphrase and summary, quoting only where wording matters
Manages time across reading, listening, planning and writing within the task limit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set a timed task with a 400-word reading and a five-minute lecture extract that challenges part of it, and ask for a 200-word response explaining how the lecture relates to the reading. Check whether the response identifies the relationship, draws selectively on both sources, transforms source wording and is organised by points rather than by source.

dependencies.reason: Learners usually sort sources by type first; understanding how peer review, preprints and grey literature are produced then explains why those types differ in status
A topic can only be narrowed appropriately once the task's scope, command words and word limit have been unpacked
Narrowing a topic requires enough background knowledge to see its sub-areas and debates
Search concepts and their combinations are derived from the focused question
Generating synonyms, narrower terms and field-specific variants depends on knowing the discipline's terminology
Using catalogues and databases effectively applies concept blocks, operators and filters
Choosing a tool depends on knowing which kinds of publication (books, articles, conference papers, grey literature) each indexes
Judgements of authority and status rest on understanding peer review, venues and versions
Source evaluation applies a questioning stance towards texts to the question of whether a text can be trusted for a purpose
Judging a source's evidence base requires knowing the kinds and relative strength of evidence
Lateral reading is a strategy for gathering the evidence about authority and purpose that evaluation requires
Lateral reading depends on fluent management of tabs, hyperlinks and search results on screen
Recognising deceptive venues and retracted work extends routine evaluation of authority and evidence
Deceptive journals exploit the author-pays open-access model, which needs to be understood first so that open access itself is not mistaken for a warning sign
Forward chaining uses the citation-linking features of databases and Google Scholar
Following references backward requires decoding reference entries written in unfamiliar systems
Choosing which references to follow is a judgement of relevance and authority
A search log records the strings, operators and filters constructed during searching
The bibliographic details that must be recorded differ by source type (chapter, article, report, web page)
Open-access routes and article versions are defined in relation to the publication process
Finding legal open versions and requesting items uses library discovery tools and services
Reproducibility depends on documenting every search and screening decision
Systematic searches run tailored strategies across several databases using their controlled vocabularies
Reviews supplement database searches with backward and forward chaining
Accurate quotation requires the conventions for quotation marks, ellipses and square brackets
Deciding whether to quote depends on what the source is doing for the writer's text
Integration operates on quotations that have already been selected and reproduced accurately
Framing a quotation uses attribution frames to introduce the source
Paraphrasing applies lexical and syntactic transformation techniques to whole propositions
Learners must understand that paraphrased ideas still require citation
A proposition cannot be restated accurately until its main clause, scope and modifiers have been parsed
Preserving a source's degree of certainty requires recognising its hedges
Word-class change depends on knowing derivational variants and the sentence slots they fit
Substitution requires judging whether near-synonyms match meaning, strength and collocation
Voice change is one of the main restructuring operations
Moving between clausal and nominal expression of a process is a key restructuring operation
Patchwriting is defined and recognised against the target of an acceptable paraphrase
The contested status of patchwriting is understood in relation to institutional definitions of plagiarism
A passage summary condenses the main idea, which must first be distinguished from supporting detail
Summaries restate the main idea in the writer's own words using reformulation operations
Summaries must be attributed to their source with signal phrases or citations
Whole-text summary builds on condensing individual passages
Applying macrorules depends on recognising the text's overall structure and signalling
Representing an author's moves (argues, reports, concludes) uses reporting verbs
Integral citation builds on attribution frames that make the cited author a sentence element
Contrasting integral and non-integral forms presupposes the mechanics of in-text citation
Attribution frames instantiate reporting structures (verb + that-clause, according to, as X notes)
Learners need to know which content requires attribution before learning how to signal it in the sentence
Marking where attributed content begins and continues uses signal phrases
Signalling boundaries applies the distinction between claims the writer avers and claims attributed to others
Boundary problems arise mainly with paraphrase and summary, which lack quotation marks to show their extent
Secondary citation formats extend standard in-text citation
The preferred alternative to secondary citation is tracing the original through backward chaining
Deciding which work is listed requires knowing how reference-list entries correspond to in-text citations
Using non-English content in English is an interlingual paraphrase that must preserve meaning and be attributed
Quoting a non-English source applies quotation conventions and adds the marking of translation
Treating sources in other languages as legitimate draws on a view of the learner's plurilingual repertoire as a resource
Referencing non-English works applies reference-list conventions for original and translated titles
Synthesis rests on the idea that sources serve the writer's purposes rather than being reported for their own sake
Learners grasp synthesis by contrast with summarising individual sources, which they need to have practised
A matrix is a tool for implementing the idea-by-idea organisation that synthesis requires
Matrix cells are condensed notes that must record source details and keep source content separate from own comment
Filling a row requires condensing each source's aims, methods and findings
Reading a matrix down its columns is a common route to discovering cross-source themes
Grouping sources applies the logic of classification by explicit criteria
Grouping sources around question-relevant themes presupposes reading selectively in relation to the writing task
Relationships are articulated between sources that address the same theme or point
Writing relationships presupposes having compared and corroborated claims across texts while reading
Relating sources draws on the language of similarity and difference
Tensions and gaps become visible once agreement, extension and contradiction between sources have been articulated
Many gaps and conflicts are explained by differences or limitations in samples, designs and measures
Claiming a gap credibly requires an overview of the field's themes, debates and key authors
Synthesis paragraphs are built from explicit relationships between sources
A synthesis paragraph is controlled by a topic sentence expressing the writer's point
Multi-source paragraphs require clear boundaries between each source and the writer's commentary
Grouping and contrasting sources depends on choosing information-prominent and author-prominent citation forms
Integrated tasks require condensing source content in the writer's own words
Many integrated tasks require relating sources to one another rather than summarising each
Integrated tasks apply, under task constraints, the general process of moving from source notes to the writer's own text
Listening-to-writing tasks require notes that preserve the structure and stance of spoken input
Strategies for integrated tasks depend on knowing the specific task structure and constraints of the test
Integrated test responses are produced under strict time limits and draw on rapid planning and time allocation

guidance.summary: Teach classification as reasoning rather than labelling: whether a source is primary, secondary or tertiary depends on the question and discipline, and the distinction between empirical, review and theoretical work can be read from genre signals such as abstracts, methods headings and reference lists. The ACRL frame 'Information Creation as a Process' supplies the rationale: format reflects how information was produced and therefore what it can support. Wallace and Wray's distinction between theoretical, research, practice and policy literature is a useful extension for learners bound for postgraduate study.

activities.title: Source sort with a discipline switch
learnerActions: In pairs, sort ten first pages or screenshots into primary, secondary and tertiary for a history question
Re-sort the same set for a public health question and mark which items changed category
Write one sentence for each changed item explaining why its status depends on the question
activities.intendedInsight: Source type is a relation between a source and a question, not a fixed property of the document.
activities.rationale: Classifying the same set for two purposes directs attention to function rather than format, the central move in the ACRL creation-process frame.

activities.title: Genre-signal hunt
learnerActions: Skim the abstracts and headings of an empirical article, a review and a theoretical paper on the same topic
Highlight the features that reveal each type (a methods heading, a statement that the paper reviews studies, the absence of data)
Use these features to classify three new abstracts and compare decisions with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Text-internal signals show what kind of knowledge a source offers before it is read in full.
activities.rationale: Learners often rely on where a source was found; attention to the text's own features transfers to unfamiliar sources and supports later reading decisions.

difficulties.pattern: If it is on the library website, it must be an academic source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists that include magazine features, trade press or newspaper items found through the discovery layer and used as scholarly evidence
difficulties.response: Show that discovery tools index many document types and have learners filter by type and check the venue. Do not ban non-scholarly sources; ask what each was used to support.

difficulties.pattern: A primary source is the main or most important source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners label a key review article 'primary' or use 'primary' to mean 'central'
difficulties.response: Contrast the everyday and disciplinary senses explicitly, with field-specific examples: a diary in history, an interview dataset in sociology, an original experiment in the sciences.

difficulties.pattern: Theoretical papers have no data, so they are just opinion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conceptual articles dismissed as 'not evidence' or treated as equivalent to blog posts
difficulties.response: Explain that theoretical work supplies the concepts and frameworks that organise evidence, and model citing such sources for definitions and frameworks rather than for findings.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a sociology journal article that includes interview extracts, a systematic review and a newspaper report of one of the reviewed studies. Ask them to classify each and say what each could support in an essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Classifies with reference to the question and discipline, notes that the interview extracts are primary data reported within a secondary article, and assigns suitable uses: the review for an overview of evidence, the news report for public framing of the issue.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Classifies correctly by format but cannot say what each could support, or treats the news report as equivalent evidence to the review.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Classifies by where the item was found or by length and treats all three as interchangeable evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on scholarly versus popular and on reading genre signals in textbooks and journal articles. On pre-sessional courses, link source types to what tutors accept in an extended essay. In undergraduate in-sessional work, make disciplinary variation explicit, especially in history, law and the arts, where primary sources have specific meanings (see dhu.primary-sources).

guidance.summary: Present scholarly publishing as a social process through which disciplinary communities check, contest and record knowledge, drawing on Swales's account of discourse communities and Hyland's of disciplinary interaction. The aim is calibrated trust: peer review filters but does not guarantee, preprints are valuable but provisional, and fields privilege different outlets. Learners use this understanding when evaluating sources, choosing which version to cite and, later, when publishing themselves.

activities.title: Follow one study through the system
learnerActions: Track a single study from preprint or conference abstract to published article using links on the preprint server and journal site
Note what changed between versions (title, sample, conclusions, strength of claims)
Decide which version to cite in an essay and justify the choice in two sentences
activities.intendedInsight: A study can exist in several versions, and the published version reflects changes made through review.
activities.rationale: Tracing a concrete case makes an abstract process visible and ties it to a practical citing decision.

activities.title: Field comparison of outlets
learnerActions: In discipline groups, list the main outlet types in the field (journals, monographs, conference proceedings, reports)
Ask a subject librarian or lecturer which outlets carry most prestige and why
Present a one-slide comparison to a group from another discipline
activities.intendedInsight: What counts as a high-status publication is discipline-specific.
activities.rationale: Disciplinary variation in genres and knowledge-making is well documented; consulting insiders makes tacit expectations explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Peer reviewed means proven to be true.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that present a single study's finding as established fact with boosters such as 'proves'
difficulties.response: Discuss what reviewers can and cannot check, show published findings that were later contested, and link to the language of claim calibration. Avoid swinging to the cynical view that research is unreliable.

difficulties.pattern: A preprint is the same as a published article.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations to preprint servers with no acknowledgement of their status
difficulties.response: Teach learners to read version labels, to check for a later published version and to signal preprint status when citing; discuss when citing preprints is reasonable, for example in fast-moving fields.

difficulties.pattern: In my previous studies the textbook was the authority.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy reliance on textbooks as evidence for current debates
difficulties.response: Value textbooks for consolidated knowledge and definitions, while showing the publication lag and the role of journals for current evidence. Present this as a change of purpose, not a correction of past practice.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'An article you want to use was published last month. A researcher on social media says its results are wrong. What do you do before citing it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Mentions checking for published comments, corrections or replies, considering the critic's expertise, reading the methods, and citing with appropriate hedging or noting the debate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says they would check that the journal is peer reviewed but does not engage with the specific challenge, or simply avoids the article.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes that publication settles the matter, or that the social media comment does.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need the basic system and what peer review means. Undergraduates benefit from disciplinary differences in outlets. Taught postgraduates need versions and preprints, particularly in fast-moving fields; doctoral researchers move to the author's side of the process in pub.publishing-process.

guidance.summary: Focusing bridges task analysis and searching, and it is iterative: learners propose a focus, run a trial search and adjust scope in response to what they find. The ACRL frame 'Research as Inquiry' supports treating the question as provisional. Concrete narrowing dimensions (context, population, period, variable, perspective) give learners a repeatable procedure, and checking the narrowed question against the original task prevents drift away from what was asked.

activities.title: Narrowing ladder
learnerActions: Write the broad topic at the top of the page
Add one limiting dimension per rung (context, population, period, aspect) to produce three progressively narrower questions
Run a quick trial search on each and note roughly how many relevant results appear
Choose the rung that fits the word limit and explain the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Scope is chosen by balancing answerability, the available literature and the word limit.
activities.rationale: Trial searches give immediate feedback on scope, reflecting the iterative view of inquiry in the ACRL framework.

activities.title: Brief-back check
learnerActions: Exchange focused questions with a partner, together with the original assignment brief
The partner checks whether the focused question still addresses the command words, scope and criteria
Revise the question in response
activities.intendedInsight: A focused question must remain a response to the set task.
activities.rationale: Narrowing can unintentionally change the task; checking against the brief makes this visible before reading begins.

difficulties.pattern: If I narrow it, I will not have enough to write about.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions kept very broad, producing descriptive surveys without analysis
difficulties.response: Show model essays that achieve depth on narrow questions and discuss how narrowing creates room for analysis. Do not force narrowing before the learner knows enough to see the sub-areas.

difficulties.pattern: I chose an interesting angle, but there is nothing published on it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Topics abandoned after one search, or narrowed so far that no literature exists
difficulties.response: Teach broadening moves (relaxing one dimension, using analogous contexts) and require some background reading before the question is fixed.

difficulties.pattern: My question changed the title, but it is more interesting this way.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that answer a different question from the one set
difficulties.response: Return to the brief: underline command words and scope words, and test the focused question against them.

diagnostic.task: Give the topic 'technology in education' and a 2,500-word limit. Ask the learner for a focused question and its search concepts.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a bounded, answerable question (naming, for example, a technology, a learner group and an outcome) with three distinct concepts suitable for search blocks.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Narrows in one dimension only, or lists concepts that overlap heavily.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the broad topic as a question, or produces a question that cannot be answered from literature, such as a personal prediction.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, focusing is usually done within a set title and benefits from the ladder scaffold. In-sessional undergraduates choosing project topics need help balancing interest and feasibility. For taught postgraduates focusing a dissertation, link forward to res.research-questions, where the question also shapes research design.
reviewNotes: Creswell and Creswell address research questions within research design rather than search-oriented narrowing; the citation supports the general principle of bounded, answerable questions only.

guidance.summary: Searching is a language task as well as a technical one: generating synonyms, spelling variants and broader or narrower terms draws directly on vocabulary depth and disciplinary terminology. Teach the concept-table method, Boolean logic with brackets, truncation and phrase searching, but emphasise iteration, using early results to harvest better terms. The ACRL frame 'Searching as Strategic Exploration' legitimises false starts and refinement rather than a single correct search.

activities.title: Concept table to search string
learnerActions: Split a focused question into two or three concepts in separate columns
Under each concept, list synonyms, related terms and British and American spellings, using a learner dictionary and the abstract of one relevant article
Convert the table into a search string with OR inside brackets and AND between concepts
Run it, add two terms harvested from relevant results, and compare the yield
activities.intendedInsight: Effective searches come from systematic term generation and revision based on results.
activities.rationale: Making term generation explicit addresses the vocabulary demands of searching and the iterative process the ACRL frame describes.

activities.title: Diagnose the failed search
learnerActions: Examine three failed searches: too many results, too few, and mostly irrelevant results
Identify the cause of each (missing synonyms, AND/OR confusion, over-broad truncation, a full-sentence query)
Rewrite and re-run each search
activities.intendedInsight: Search problems have identifiable causes and specific repairs.
activities.rationale: Error analysis makes the logic of operators visible and transfers to learners' own searching.

difficulties.pattern: I type my whole question into the database, as I do in a web search engine.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long natural-language queries in search histories and very few or irrelevant database results
difficulties.response: Contrast relevance-ranked web search with field-based database search by running both live. Do not say natural language never works: some discovery tools handle it, but learners need to know why many databases do not.

difficulties.pattern: There is only one word for this concept.
difficulties.revealedBy: One term per concept, sometimes a direct translation of an L1 term that is rare in English-language literature
difficulties.response: When an L1 has a single established term, learners may search with its translation equivalent and miss the variants English-language literature uses. Have them harvest terms from abstracts and subject headings of known relevant articles and check candidates in a thesaurus or corpus.

difficulties.pattern: OR gives fewer results because it is more specific.
difficulties.revealedBy: Synonyms joined with AND, producing almost no results
difficulties.response: Use Venn diagrams and live comparisons of result counts for AND and OR.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a search string for the effects of remote working on employee wellbeing, and to predict what happens if they replace OR with AND between synonyms.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces bracketed OR blocks for each concept with variants (for example remote work*, telework*, 'working from home'; wellbeing, well-being, 'mental health'), joins the blocks with AND, and correctly predicts the narrowing effect.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes some synonyms but omits spelling variants or brackets, or cannot predict the operator's effect.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes the question as a sentence or joins all terms with AND.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need keywords and simple Boolean searches in the catalogue. Pre-sessional projects are a good point to introduce concept tables. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates should apply strategies in their subject databases, including controlled vocabularies where they exist.
reviewNotes: No source in the closed bibliography reports research on L2 learners' generation of search terms; the L1-transfer difficulty is a practitioner observation.

guidance.summary: Teach tool choice by coverage: what each catalogue, discovery layer, subject database and Google Scholar indexes, and which search features each offers. Hands-on work in learners' own subject databases, ideally co-taught with subject librarians, transfers better than generic demonstrations. In terms of the ACRL strategic exploration frame, expert searchers match tools to information needs and change tools when results are poor.

activities.title: Same search, three tools
learnerActions: Run the same search string in the library discovery tool, one subject database and Google Scholar
Record result counts, the types and dates of the first ten items, and the features available (filters, subject headings, export)
Write a short recommendation on which tool suits which need
activities.intendedInsight: Tools differ in coverage and functionality, so the choice of tool affects what is found.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison makes coverage differences concrete and supports the tool-choice judgements described in the ACRL frame.

activities.title: Discovery-to-access trail
learnerActions: Locate a known book in the catalogue and note its shelf mark or e-book link
Find a peer-reviewed article in a subject database and reach the full text through the library link, on and off campus
Export both references to a reference manager or document
activities.intendedInsight: Library systems link discovery, access and record-keeping.
activities.rationale: A task chain mirrors real workflows and exposes access barriers early, before assessed work depends on them.

difficulties.pattern: Google Scholar has everything, so I do not need the databases.
difficulties.revealedBy: Searching limited to Google Scholar, with no use of subject headings or filters
difficulties.response: Acknowledge Google Scholar's strengths (breadth, citation links) and show its limitations (opaque ranking, limited filtering, mixed quality). Do not prohibit it.

difficulties.pattern: It is behind a paywall, so I cannot use it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reliance on whatever is freely available, or learners paying publishers for articles
difficulties.response: Demonstrate the library link resolver, off-campus authentication and interlibrary loan live.

difficulties.pattern: The database interface was confusing, so I gave up.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abandoned searches and reliance on one familiar tool
difficulties.response: Co-teach with subject librarians, provide a one-page guide to the main subject database and build short supported practice into class time, returning to concept blocks where the search itself is the problem.

diagnostic.task: Ask which tool the learner would use to find (a) a specific book on a reading list, (b) recent empirical studies in their field and (c) later work citing a key article, and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses the catalogue, a named subject database and a citation-linking tool respectively, with reasons based on coverage and features.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Chooses appropriately for one or two needs but defaults to a single tool for the rest.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses a general web search engine for all three.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the catalogue and discovery tool. Pre-sessional learners should practise in at least one subject database related to their destination degree. Undergraduate and postgraduate learners need discipline databases and citation indexes; doctoral researchers should also use specialist databases and alerting services.

guidance.summary: Checklists of authority, currency, relevance and purpose are useful prompts, but they can encourage surface judgements based on domain names or design; Wineburg and McGrew's comparison of fact-checkers with students and historians shows the limits of judging a source on its own terms. Teach evaluation as purpose-specific: what is this source being used to support, and is it adequate for that? Bråten and colleagues found that students' trust judgements about sources were associated with their comprehension across multiple texts, which suggests evaluation should be integrated with reading rather than taught as a separate library exercise.

activities.title: Fit for purpose
learnerActions: Receive one source and three essay purposes: illustrating public debate, supporting a causal claim, defining a concept
Decide for each purpose whether the source is adequate, and why
Compare decisions in groups and agree which criteria changed across purposes
activities.intendedInsight: A source is credible for something, not credible in general.
activities.rationale: Holding the source constant while changing the purpose shows evaluation as contextual judgement, as the ACRL authority frame describes.

activities.title: Beyond the checklist
learnerActions: Apply a standard checklist to a well-designed website from an organisation with an undeclared interest and record the verdict
Investigate the organisation laterally for five minutes
Compare the two verdicts and note what the checklist missed
activities.intendedInsight: Surface features can mislead; evidence from outside the source often decides credibility.
activities.rationale: Wineburg and McGrew observed that vertical, within-site reading led students and historians to trust sites that fact-checkers quickly identified as problematic.

difficulties.pattern: Sites ending in .org, or with a reference list, are reliable.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluation justifications that cite domain, design or the mere presence of references
difficulties.response: Show counter-examples and teach checking who funds the organisation and whether the references actually support the claims. Do not replace one rule of thumb with another.

difficulties.pattern: If a source agrees with my argument, it is a good source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical use of supportive sources alongside harsh critique of opposing ones
difficulties.response: Ask learners to apply the same criteria to a source they disagree with, and link evaluation to the questioning stance of critical reading.

difficulties.pattern: I cannot judge experts; I am only a student.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to make any evaluative comment about published work
difficulties.response: Frame evaluation as asking reasonable questions about fit, evidence and interests rather than judging expertise, and provide frames for tentative evaluation.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a company press release announcing that a study shows its product improves memory, and the abstract of the underlying study. Ask whether and how each could be used in an essay on cognitive enhancement.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the commercial interest, checks what the study measured and with whom, notes any gap between the abstract and the press release, and limits use accordingly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes the company's interest but uses the press release's figures without checking the study.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses the press release as evidence for the claim without comment.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, focus on scholarly versus non-scholarly sources and purpose-specific use. In-sessional undergraduates should apply module-specific expectations. For taught postgraduates, evaluation increasingly merges with methods critique (rdc.methods-critique).

guidance.summary: Wineburg and McGrew found that professional fact-checkers left unfamiliar websites quickly, read across other sources to establish who was behind them, and practised 'click restraint' when choosing search results, whereas historians and students read vertically within the site and were more often misled. Teach lateral reading as a short, habitual routine for unfamiliar web sources, organisations and statistics. It complements, rather than replaces, close reading of a source once its provenance is established.

activities.title: Vertical versus lateral
learnerActions: In pairs, one learner evaluates an unfamiliar site by reading it; the other leaves the site at once and searches for information about its publisher
After five minutes, both report a verdict and the evidence used
Swap roles on a second site and discuss which approach was faster and better informed
activities.intendedInsight: Information about a source from other sources is often more diagnostic than the source itself.
activities.rationale: The task reproduces the contrast between vertical and lateral reading documented by Wineburg and McGrew.

activities.title: Trace the statistic
learnerActions: Take a statistic quoted in a news article or social media post
Follow links and searches to its original source
Record whether the original supports the claim as reported and how it was changed
activities.intendedInsight: Claims change as they travel; checking the origin is part of evaluation.
activities.rationale: Tracing claims upstream is part of the fact-checking repertoire and builds the habit of checking before citing.

difficulties.pattern: Leaving the page feels like not reading carefully.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners spend all the available time reading the site itself before any external check
