difficulties.response: Distinguish purposes: close reading is for understanding content; lateral reading establishes whether to trust the source first. Model and time the routine.

difficulties.pattern: I clicked the first result about the organisation, which was its own page.
difficulties.revealedBy: Search histories showing reliance on top-ranked results or on the organisation's own materials
difficulties.response: Teach click restraint: scan the results page, prefer independent coverage and reference works, and check where each result comes from.

difficulties.pattern: We were told never to use Wikipedia, so I cannot look there.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners avoid reference works entirely, even for orientation
difficulties.response: Distinguish using an encyclopaedia to find out about an organisation or topic from citing it as evidence; Wineburg and McGrew report fact-checkers using it in this way.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a link to an unfamiliar organisation's report and five minutes to decide whether to cite it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Leaves the site promptly, establishes the organisation's funding, stance and reputation from independent sources, and decides on use with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Checks the 'About' page and perhaps one external source but bases the decision mainly on the site's self-presentation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges from design, domain or tone without any external check.

guidance.contextNotes: Lateral reading is accessible from foundation level because searching for an organisation's name is linguistically light. It matters most when learners use web sources, policy reports and media. At postgraduate level, apply it to unfamiliar journals and publishers (see inf.problematic-publishing).
reviewNotes: Wineburg and McGrew's participants were US-based; specific checks (for example which reference sites are useful) may need adapting to other information environments.

guidance.summary: Learners need a small set of verification habits rather than lists of 'bad journals': verify a venue's claims about indexing, editorial board and review against independent sources, check an article's status for corrections and retractions, and trace widely repeated claims to their origin. Definitions of 'predatory' publishing are contested and no universal list is reliable, so teach indicators and verification rather than blacklists. Fabricated references produced by generative AI tools are a newer route by which non-existent work enters student writing.

activities.title: Venue verification
learnerActions: Read an unsolicited invitation from a journal and visit its website
List the claims it makes about indexing, metrics and peer review
Verify each claim with an independent source, such as the claimed index's own title list
Decide whether to cite from or submit to the journal, giving reasons
activities.intendedInsight: Venue claims must be verified independently, not accepted at face value.
activities.rationale: Applying lateral checks to journals transfers an established evaluation habit to scholarly venues, where indicators are debated.

activities.title: Retraction check
learnerActions: Look up a set of articles, including one known retracted article, in a database and on the publisher's site
Find the retraction or correction notice and summarise what it says
Discuss why the article may still be cited and what a writer should do
activities.intendedInsight: Published work can be withdrawn, so status must be checked before citing.
activities.rationale: Seeing notices in situ makes the concept concrete and builds a routine check.

difficulties.pattern: The journal says it is indexed and has an impact factor, so it is fine.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations to, or planned submissions to, journals whose claims cannot be verified
difficulties.response: Show how to check claims in the indexes themselves and discuss misleading metrics, building on the evaluation routine learners already use for other sources.

difficulties.pattern: Open-access journals are all predatory.
difficulties.revealedBy: Exclusion of reputable open-access sources
difficulties.response: Separate business model from quality: show reputable open-access journals and explain that author charges are not in themselves a warning sign.

difficulties.pattern: The AI tool gave me these references, so they exist.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists containing plausible but non-existent articles
difficulties.response: Require every reference to be located in a library tool before it is cited, and connect to gai.verifying-output. Treat this first as a verification skill to be taught, while being clear about institutional rules.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a plausible-looking reference that has been retracted and a second reference in a journal with doubtful indexing claims. Ask whether they would cite each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds the retraction notice, verifies the indexing claims independently and decides not to cite either as evidence (or cites the retraction itself if discussing it), with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Detects one problem but not the other, or relies on the journal's own website for verification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cites both without checking.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional and undergraduate programmes, focus on article status, misinformation and fabricated references. Taught postgraduates and doctoral researchers also need venue verification when citing and, at PGR level, when choosing where to publish (see pub.journal-selection).
reviewNotes: grudniewicz2019 is a proposed reference and must be verified before publication; if it is removed, the statement that definitions of predatory publishing are contested needs another source.

guidance.summary: Chaining puts the ACRL frame 'Scholarship as Conversation' into practice: references point back to the conversation a source joined, and 'cited by' links show how it continued. It is particularly efficient for learners whose keyword searching is limited by vocabulary, because one relevant source leads to others regardless of terminology. Learners should chain selectively, choosing references by how the citing text uses them, and record the links to see the shape of a debate.

activities.title: Read the reference in context
learnerActions: Choose a relevant article and highlight each sentence in its introduction that cites other work
Classify what each citation is used for (key finding, method, contrasting view, background)
Select three references to follow and justify each choice by its use in the text
activities.intendedInsight: How a reference is used in the citing text shows whether it is worth following.
activities.rationale: Selecting by function rather than position in the list makes chaining purposeful and reflects the conversational view of scholarship.

activities.title: Forward from a key study
learnerActions: Find a well-known study in the field in a citation index or Google Scholar
Use 'cited by' to list citing works and filter to the last five years
Skim abstracts and classify whether each supports, extends or challenges the original
activities.intendedInsight: Forward chaining shows how a claim has fared since publication.
activities.rationale: Tracking uptake supports judgements of currency and prepares for synthesising agreement and disagreement.

difficulties.pattern: I followed every reference in the list and drowned.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large, unmanaged collections of loosely relevant sources
difficulties.response: Limit chaining to references used substantively in the citing text and to two generations, applying relevance and authority judgements at each step.

difficulties.pattern: I cannot find the cited item from the reference.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abandoned references, especially in numeric or note-based systems
difficulties.response: Model decoding entries in unfamiliar styles and searching by title in the catalogue.

difficulties.pattern: Older references are out of date and can be ignored.
difficulties.revealedBy: Foundational works rejected because of their date
difficulties.response: Distinguish foundational works that define a field from superseded findings; forward chaining shows whether a work is still cited and how.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner one relevant article and fifteen minutes. Ask for two backward and two forward sources, each with a one-line reason.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects sources from substantive citations, uses a citation index for forward chaining, and gives relevance-based reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds sources but selects arbitrarily or chains only backward.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot locate cited items or does not know that forward chaining is possible.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, chaining from a key reading supplements limited keyword searching. Undergraduates should chain from module reading lists. Taught postgraduates and doctoral researchers should chain systematically and record links, which feeds literature mapping (rdc.literature-mapping) and synthesis.

guidance.summary: Record-keeping has low status but high consequences: incomplete records lead to unverifiable citations, wasted repeat searching and, when the origin of a note is lost, unattributed borrowing. Teach a minimal search log and the habit of capturing complete bibliographic details and locators at the point of reading, using a reference manager where available. The ACRL strategic exploration frame includes managing searching processes and results.

activities.title: Search log replication
learnerActions: Set up a log with columns for date, tool, search string, filters and results
Log every search during a 30-minute session
Swap logs with a partner, who tries to re-run two searches from the log alone
activities.intendedInsight: A search is reproducible only if it is recorded in enough detail.
activities.rationale: Peer replication gives an immediate, concrete test of record quality.

activities.title: Note-to-source audit
learnerActions: Take five notes made in the previous week
For each, identify the exact source and page or other locator
Repair any note that cannot be traced and agree a recording routine
activities.intendedInsight: Notes that cannot be traced to a source put accurate citation at risk.
activities.rationale: Auditing real notes ties record-keeping to accurate source use rather than presenting it as administration.

difficulties.pattern: I will remember where I read it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations without page numbers or details, and time spent re-finding sources near deadlines
difficulties.response: Let learners experience the cost of re-finding a source, then introduce recording at the point of reading. Do not mandate one tool; prioritise a consistent routine.

difficulties.pattern: The reference manager does it all for me.
difficulties.revealedBy: Imported records with missing or wrong fields used without checking, for example chapters recorded as books
difficulties.response: Show common import errors and build in a check of each record against the source, attending to the fields each source type requires.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show the record of a source used last week and the search that found it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces complete bibliographic details, a locator for the note, and a log entry sufficient to re-run the search.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has bibliographic details but no locator or search record.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify where the information came from.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on recording full references and page numbers. Pre-sessional and undergraduate learners should add search logs for projects. For dissertations and doctoral work, link record-keeping to reference managers (dig.reference-managers) and systematic searching.
reviewNotes: The link between lost source records and unintentional plagiarism is widely asserted in practitioner guidance; no source in the closed bibliography is cited for it here.

guidance.summary: Access to scholarship is structured by publishing business models and copyright, which the ACRL frame 'Information Has Value' asks learners to understand. Practically, learners need the legitimate routes to paywalled work and the ability to identify which version they have found. Discussion of unauthorised download sites should be factual rather than moralising, acknowledging the inequities of access that many learners have experienced.

activities.title: Legal access challenge
learnerActions: Receive three references to paywalled articles
Obtain each by a legitimate route: library subscription, repository, open-access finder, interlibrary loan or author request
Record the route used and the version found
activities.intendedInsight: Most paywalled work can be obtained legitimately with the right routes.
activities.rationale: Practising the legitimate routes is intended to reduce reliance on unauthorised sources (an untested expectation) and links access to version awareness.

activities.title: Who pays?
learnerActions: Compare how a subscription journal, an open-access journal with author charges, an open-access journal without author charges and a repository are funded
Discuss who can read and who can publish under each model
Relate the discussion to access in learners' home or previous institutions
activities.intendedInsight: Access models distribute costs and opportunities unequally.
activities.rationale: Understanding the value of information is a knowledge practice in the ACRL framework and prepares learners to recognise deceptive venues.

difficulties.pattern: If it is free to read, it must be lower quality.
difficulties.revealedBy: Exclusion of open-access sources
difficulties.response: Show reputable open-access journals and explain that peer review is independent of the access model.

difficulties.pattern: Everyone uses those download sites; there is no other way.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report unauthorised download sites as their default route
difficulties.response: Acknowledge access inequities without judgement, demonstrate the legitimate routes now available to them, and explain the legal and security risks. Avoid moralising.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain two legitimate ways to obtain a paywalled article and how to tell whether a free PDF is the published version.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names library access, repositories or interlibrary loan, and identifies the version from labelling, layout and comparison with the publisher's landing page.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names one route and is unsure about versions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Knows no legitimate route other than paying.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners need the basic legal routes. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates need version awareness for citing. Doctoral researchers need open-access options and funder requirements for their own publications.

guidance.summary: Systematic and scoping searches differ from everyday searching in their transparency and reproducibility: a protocol, explicit criteria, full strategies and a record of decisions. Reporting guidelines such as PRISMA 2020 for systematic reviews, and methodological frameworks for scoping studies, set out what must be reported. Teach the procedure with subject librarians, and make clear that many taught dissertations require a documented, structured search rather than a full systematic review.

activities.title: Protocol in miniature
learnerActions: Write a one-page protocol for a dissertation question: question, databases, concept table, search strings, criteria
Run the strategy in one database and record the results
Ask a peer to run it, compare results and revise ambiguous elements
activities.intendedInsight: Reproducibility is tested by someone else running the strategy.
activities.rationale: Peer replication puts into practice the transparency standard that reporting guidelines set.

activities.title: Screening calibration
learnerActions: Two learners independently screen the same twenty abstracts against agreed criteria
Compare decisions and discuss disagreements
Reword the criteria to reduce ambiguity
activities.intendedInsight: Criteria must be explicit enough to be applied consistently by different people.
activities.rationale: Independent screening and calibration are standard review practice and reveal where criteria are underspecified.

difficulties.pattern: Systematic just means I searched thoroughly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dissertations that claim a systematic review without strategies, criteria or a flow of records
difficulties.response: Distinguish systematic, scoping and narrative reviews and what each requires, and help learners choose an accurate label for what they did.

difficulties.pattern: I changed my criteria after reading the papers and did not note it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent inclusion and unexplained exclusions
difficulties.response: Allow principled revision but require every change and its reason to be documented.

difficulties.pattern: Writing such long strings in database syntax is overwhelming.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strategies abandoned or oversimplified
difficulties.response: Build strings incrementally from the concept table with librarian support, testing each block separately.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe how another researcher could reproduce their literature search.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes full strategies per database, dates, criteria, the screening process and records kept, and names the field's reporting guideline.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes databases and keywords but not criteria or screening records.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot describe the search beyond naming one search engine.

guidance.contextNotes: This topic serves mainly taught postgraduates and doctoral researchers in fields with an evidence-synthesis tradition, and final-year undergraduates in health disciplines. Match expectations to the assignment: many taught dissertations require a structured, documented search rather than a full systematic review.
reviewNotes: page2021prisma and arksey2005 are proposed references and need verification before publication.

guidance.summary: Treat quotation as a deliberate choice governed by discipline-dependent norms. Hyland's cross-disciplinary analysis found direct quotation concentrated in the humanities and social sciences and very rare in the sciences, so a single rule ('quote sparingly' or 'never quote') misleads some learners. Teach criteria for when wording matters, then precision: exact reproduction, economical selection, correctly marked omissions and insertions, and locators. Pecorari argues that good source use needs explicit, repeated teaching, and quotation is an accessible starting point.

activities.title: Quote or not?
learnerActions: Read six candidate extracts from a source
Decide for each whether to quote, paraphrase or summarise, using criteria (distinctive wording, definition, object of analysis, routine information)
Justify two decisions to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Quotation is warranted when the wording itself matters.
activities.rationale: Explicit criteria counter both over-quotation and blanket avoidance, and can be tied to disciplinary norms.

activities.title: Trim and mark
learnerActions: Take a long quotation from a sample essay
Shorten it to the essential words using ellipses and square brackets
Check with a partner that the trimmed version has not changed the meaning
activities.intendedInsight: Economical quotation requires exact marking of changes without distorting the source.
activities.rationale: Practising omission and insertion conventions builds accuracy and economy together.

difficulties.pattern: Quoting is safest because then nobody can accuse me of plagiarism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays composed largely of long quotations with little commentary
difficulties.response: Acknowledge the anxiety, then show how over-quotation hides the writer's understanding and voice. Do not ban quotation; agree criteria and a proportion appropriate to the discipline, returning to what each source is meant to do.

difficulties.pattern: I changed a few words inside the quotation to make it fit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotation marks around wording that differs from the source
difficulties.response: Teach that quotation marks guarantee exact wording, and show how to use square brackets or change the surrounding frame instead.

difficulties.pattern: In my previous studies we always quoted the authority.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy quotation in a target discipline where it is unusual, such as engineering
difficulties.response: Compare expert texts from the learner's target discipline and discuss its norms, without implying that previous practice was wrong.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a paragraph that quotes a routine statistic and paraphrases a distinctive definition. Ask whether they would change anything.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Recommends paraphrasing the statistic and quoting the definition, with reasons about whether the wording matters.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises one of the two problems.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no issue, or prefers to quote everything.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on accuracy and the mechanics of short quotations. Pre-sessional learners should practise selection criteria and economy. Undergraduates should calibrate frequency to their discipline: quotation is central in literary studies and law but rare in many sciences.

guidance.summary: Effective quotation needs a frame before it and commentary after it: the frame names the source and indicates its relevance or stance, and the commentary explains what the quotation shows for the writer's point. Petrić's finding that stronger theses used citations for more than attribution supports teaching the follow-up move explicitly. Grammatical integration of partial quotations is a frequent site of error and benefits from focused practice.

activities.title: Frame and follow-up repair
learnerActions: Identify dropped quotations in a sample essay
Add an introductory frame naming the source and its relevance
Add one or two sentences interpreting each quotation and linking it to the paragraph's claim
activities.intendedInsight: A quotation becomes evidence only when the writer frames and interprets it.
activities.rationale: Explicit attention to the follow-up move addresses the tendency for citations to be used for attribution only.

activities.title: Make it fit
learnerActions: Combine given partial quotations with given frames
Read each combined sentence aloud without the quotation marks to check its grammar
Repair errors by changing the frame, not the quoted words
activities.intendedInsight: The writer's frame must adapt to the quotation's grammar.
activities.rationale: Reading without the quotation marks exposes syntactic mismatches that learners otherwise overlook.

difficulties.pattern: The quotation speaks for itself.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that end on a quotation with no comment
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to write what the quotation shows for their argument; if they cannot, revisit whether a quotation is needed at all.

difficulties.pattern: The author argues that 'the results is consistent with'... (frame and quotation do not fit).
difficulties.revealedBy: Ungrammatical sentences at the join between frame and quotation
difficulties.response: Practise reading the combined sentence without quotation marks and identifying which clause element the quotation must supply. Do not alter the quoted words to repair the sentence.

difficulties.pattern: I always write 'X says that' before a quotation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive frames that give no signal of relevance or stance
difficulties.response: Once basic framing is secure, extend the range of frames and link to reporting verbs; avoid encouraging variation for its own sake.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to integrate a given 25-word quotation into a paragraph supporting a given claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Introduces the source with a relevant frame, quotes only what is needed, integrates it grammatically and adds interpretation tied to the claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Frames and quotes correctly but adds no interpretation, or the interpretation only repeats the quotation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Drops the quotation without a frame or creates a grammatical mismatch.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need the frame–quotation–commentary pattern and grammatical integration. Undergraduates in the humanities need finer integration of short phrases within analytical sentences. For taught postgraduates the emphasis is on interpretive commentary that advances an argument.
reviewNotes: Petrić's study supports the value of citations performing functions beyond attribution; it did not test the frame-and-follow-up technique itself.

guidance.summary: Research suggests that L2 writers' close dependence on source wording is often developmental and tied to comprehension and available linguistic resources (Pecorari; Shi; Keck), and that learners may experience paraphrasing as a mechanical requirement rather than a way of understanding and using sources (Hirvela and Du). Teach paraphrase as comprehension-driven reformulation: understand the idea, set the source aside, write from memory or notes, then check against the source for meaning, certainty and copied strings. Treat early attempts that stay close to the source as stages to work through with formative feedback, and make local expectations explicit, since academics themselves do not fully agree on where acceptable paraphrase ends.

activities.title: Cover, write, check
learnerActions: Read a short passage until you can explain its point to a partner without looking
Cover the passage and write the idea in your own words for a stated purpose
Uncover it, underline any strings of three or more words shared with the source, and check meaning, scope and hedging
Revise and add a citation
activities.intendedInsight: Paraphrase starts from understanding, not from editing the source sentence.
activities.rationale: Writing without the source in view is widely recommended to reduce reliance on source structure, and the check makes retained wording visible. This is a proposal rather than a tested intervention.

activities.title: Why paraphrase here?
learnerActions: Choose a paraphrase in your own draft
Explain to a partner what the paraphrased idea does for your argument
Rewrite the paraphrase so that it foregrounds the aspect your paragraph will discuss
activities.intendedInsight: Paraphrase serves the writer's purpose and can be shaped to the argument.
activities.rationale: Hirvela and Du found that students who approached paraphrasing as a display requirement did not connect it to their own understanding or argument; linking paraphrase to purpose addresses this.

difficulties.pattern: I changed every few words, so it is in my own words now.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that keep the source's sentence structure with synonyms substituted
difficulties.response: Show source and paraphrase side by side with shared strings highlighted, and teach the cover-and-write routine. At early stages, do not treat this as misconduct; give formative feedback and repeated practice.

difficulties.pattern: I cannot paraphrase this sentence; it is too difficult.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that copy or distort the difficult part of a sentence
difficulties.response: Check comprehension first by asking the learner to identify the main clause and explain the idea orally. If comprehension is the problem, more paraphrase practice will not help until the reading difficulty is addressed.

difficulties.pattern: The source said 'may', but I wrote 'shows' because it is clearer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that increase or reduce the source's certainty
difficulties.response: Treat certainty as part of meaning: highlight hedges in the source and require them to be matched in strength.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 60-word passage containing a hedged claim and a technical term. Ask for a paraphrase written with the source covered.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Preserves meaning, certainty and scope; changes structure and vocabulary; keeps the technical term; includes a citation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Preserves meaning but keeps the source structure or several strings, or drops the hedge or the citation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies with minor substitutions, distorts the meaning or omits attribution.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, keep source texts short and accessible and expect close dependence on source wording as part of development. Pre-sessional learners paraphrase under time pressure and in assessed writing and need formative feedback before summative judgement. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates paraphrase disciplinary texts, where keeping technical terms and precise scope is critical.
reviewNotes: shi2012 is a proposed reference, cited for disagreement among instructors about acceptable paraphrase; if it is not verified, the final sentence of the summary should be softened or re-sourced.

guidance.summary: Techniques give learners concrete operations, but taught alone they can encourage the mechanical substitution that produces patchwriting. Keck's taxonomy, which classifies paraphrases by the extent of retained source wording from near copy to substantial revision, offers a shared language for feedback. Teach techniques as tools within a comprehension-first process, with explicit attention to their limits: near-synonyms shift meaning, and technical terms should be kept.

activities.title: One sentence, five ways
learnerActions: Take one source sentence
Rewrite it using a specified operation each time (word-class change, voice change, clause reordering, nominalisation, combining with the next sentence)
Judge which versions preserve the meaning and which read naturally in context
activities.intendedInsight: Each operation changes something different, and not every change preserves meaning or reads well.
activities.rationale: Isolated practice builds the lexicogrammatical repertoire paraphrase requires before it is combined with comprehension-based writing; Keck's categories give a way to judge the result.

activities.title: Synonym trap
learnerActions: Look up suggested synonyms for three words in a source sentence in a learner dictionary or corpus
Test each in the sentence for meaning, strength and collocation
Identify any word that should not be replaced because it is a technical term
activities.intendedInsight: Synonyms are rarely exact, and some words should be kept.
activities.rationale: Making near-synonym differences explicit addresses meaning distortion, a typical outcome when substitution is the main strategy.

difficulties.pattern: The thesaurus gives me words with the same meaning.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unidiomatic or meaning-changing substitutions
difficulties.response: Teach checking candidates for collocation and register in a learner dictionary or corpus. Do not ban thesauri; show how to verify their suggestions.

difficulties.pattern: Changing it to the passive makes it different enough.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that change voice only and keep the rest of the source sentence
difficulties.response: Show that a single operation leaves the source structure recognisable, and combine operations with writing from understanding.

difficulties.pattern: I do not know the noun form of this verb.
difficulties.revealedBy: Word-form errors in attempted transformations, such as 'the analyse of'
difficulties.response: Provide focused word-family work on high-frequency academic words used in the learners' sources.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a sentence and ask for two different transformations, naming the operation used in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces two accurate transformations using different operations, preserving meaning and keeping technical terms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces transformations with minor word-form or collocation errors, or slight shifts in meaning.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Produces only one-word substitutions or ungrammatical sentences.

guidance.contextNotes: Techniques are most useful at foundation and early pre-sessional stages, while linguistic resources are developing. By the in-sessional stage, emphasis should move to integrated paraphrase in writing, with techniques revisited to address specific problems.

guidance.summary: Howard characterised patchwriting as copying from a source while deleting words, altering grammatical structures or substituting synonyms, and argued that it is a transitional strategy used when writers do not yet fully understand a text, so it calls for teaching rather than punishment. Pecorari's study of postgraduate L2 writers found extensive patchwriting without apparent intent to deceive, and Pennycook showed that notions of textual ownership are historically and culturally situated. Present patchwriting to learners as a recognisable stage with strategies for moving beyond it, while being honest that institutional policies may still classify it as plagiarism.

activities.title: Find the patches
learnerActions: Compare a source paragraph with a patchwritten version
Highlight retained strings and parallel structures in matching colours
Place the version on a simple scale (near copy, minimal revision, substantial revision)
Rewrite one sentence as a genuine paraphrase and another as a marked quotation
activities.intendedInsight: Patchwriting is visible in shared strings and structure, and it can be repaired by paraphrasing or by quoting.
activities.rationale: Side-by-side comparison makes textual dependence visible; the scale adapts Keck's categories of paraphrase.

activities.title: Policy and practice
learnerActions: Read the institution's definition of plagiarism
Decide whether given examples of close paraphrase with citation fall within it
Discuss why Howard and Pecorari argue that patchwriting should be treated developmentally, and what that means for your own drafting
activities.intendedInsight: Patchwriting sits in a contested space between learning strategy and policy breach.
activities.rationale: Discussing the contested status makes expectations explicit and can reduce anxiety without misrepresenting institutional rules.

difficulties.pattern: I cited it, so it cannot be plagiarism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Close copying with a citation and no quotation marks
difficulties.response: Explain that a citation attributes the idea and quotation marks attribute the wording; both are needed when wording is retained. Return to what an acceptable paraphrase changes.

difficulties.pattern: I am afraid anything I write from sources will be called plagiarism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of sources, or excessive quotation
difficulties.response: Frame patchwriting as a normal stage, offer low-stakes practice with formative feedback, and clarify how the institution's definitions apply. Avoid fear-based integrity messages.

difficulties.pattern: Copying good sentences is how I learned to write well.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memorised sentences from sources reproduced without marking
difficulties.response: Acknowledge imitation and memorisation as legitimate learning strategies, and distinguish reusing general academic phrases ('it has been argued that') from reproducing a source's specific wording. Pennycook's discussion of memory and ownership supports a non-judgemental approach.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a cited passage that closely follows its source, and ask whether it is acceptable and how to fix it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies retained strings and structure, explains that a citation alone is insufficient for borrowed wording, and revises into a paraphrase or quotation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices the similarity but cannot explain why it matters or how to fix it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges it acceptable because it is cited.

guidance.contextNotes: Patchwriting is expected and should be addressed developmentally at foundation and pre-sessional stages. For undergraduates and taught postgraduates, connect it to institutional policy and to similarity reports (int.similarity-reports). Pecorari's participants were postgraduates, so doctoral researchers writing in a second language may still patchwrite, especially in dense theoretical or technical prose.
reviewNotes: The status of patchwriting is contested; institutional definitions differ, and some treat it as plagiarism regardless of intent. Activities are proposals rather than tested interventions.

guidance.summary: Passage summary builds the main-idea identification and reformulation that whole-text summary and synthesis depend on. Johns and Mayes found that lower-proficiency university ESL students copied more directly and combined fewer idea units, and Keck found that L2 writers used more near copies than L1 writers when paraphrasing in summaries, so the language demand of summarising should not be underestimated. Teach selection first (what to keep), then condensed reformulation, then checking against the source for meaning and borrowed wording.

activities.title: Main idea in ten words
learnerActions: Read a paragraph and underline the words that carry its main idea
Cross out examples, repetition and minor details
Write the main idea in no more than ten words without looking at the paragraph
Expand it into a 25-word attributed summary, keeping any qualification that affects meaning
activities.intendedInsight: Summary starts with deciding what matters, then expressing it in new words.
activities.rationale: Separating selection from reformulation reduces the load that tends to produce copying, a pattern Johns and Mayes observed in lower-proficiency summarisers.

activities.title: Summary comparison
learnerActions: Read three summaries of the same paragraph: one copied, one distorted, one acceptable
Identify the problems in each
Agree class criteria for a good summary and use them to check your own
activities.intendedInsight: Good summaries are accurate, condensed, reformulated and attributed.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples help learners build criteria for self-assessment.

difficulties.pattern: I copy the topic sentence because it is the main idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that reproduce topic sentences verbatim
difficulties.response: Credit the correct identification, then require reformulation from memory. At foundation level, give formative feedback rather than penalising heavily.

difficulties.pattern: Everything in the paragraph seems important.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries nearly as long as the source, including examples
difficulties.response: Practise separating main ideas from support through paragraph-structure analysis before summarising.

difficulties.pattern: I forgot to say whose ideas they were.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed summaries in essays
difficulties.response: Require a signal phrase or citation in every practice summary until it becomes automatic.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 120-word paragraph and ask for a one-sentence summary written without looking back.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Captures the main idea and any key qualification in own words, with attribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures the main idea but copies phrases or omits attribution.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises a detail or example rather than the main idea, or copies a sentence.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, use short, accessible paragraphs and textbook extracts. On pre-sessional courses, practise summary within note-making and integrated tasks. For undergraduates, passage summary feeds whole-text summary and synthesis.

guidance.summary: Brown and Day's macrorules (deletion, superordination, selection and invention of topic statements) and Kintsch and van Dijk's model of macrostructure describe what expert summarisers do: they build a representation of the text's gist rather than shortening each paragraph in turn. Brown and Day also found that the most demanding rule, inventing a topic statement, develops late. Teach learners to identify the text's purpose and structure first, then apply macrorules section by section, and to represent the author's moves with reporting language.

activities.title: Macrorules walkthrough
learnerActions: Preview the title, abstract, headings and conclusion to identify the text's purpose and structure
For each section, delete trivial and repeated material, replace lists with superordinate terms and write one gist statement
Combine the gist statements into a summary, adjusting proportions to the text's emphasis
Add reporting verbs that show the author's moves
activities.intendedInsight: Whole-text summary is built from the text's macrostructure, not its paragraph sequence.
activities.rationale: The procedure operationalises Brown and Day's macrorules and Kintsch and van Dijk's account of macrostructure.

activities.title: Purpose-shaped summaries
learnerActions: Write a 50-word summary of an article for an annotated bibliography
Write a 100-word summary of the same article for an essay's background section, focused on one aspect
Compare what was included in each and why
activities.intendedInsight: Summaries are shaped by purpose and length.
activities.rationale: Varying the purpose shows summary as a selective, rhetorical act rather than neutral reduction.

difficulties.pattern: I summarise each paragraph in order, one sentence each.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that follow the source's paragraph order and give equal weight to minor sections
difficulties.response: Teach previewing and identification of the text's macrostructure before summarising, with a gist template (purpose, method or approach, main findings or argument, conclusion).

difficulties.pattern: I added my opinion to show I understood it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluative comments mixed into summaries without marking
difficulties.response: Clarify that a summary represents the author's view and that evaluation belongs in a separate, signalled section unless the task combines them.

difficulties.pattern: The author says… then the author says…
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated 'says' that misrepresents the author's moves
difficulties.response: Once macrostructure is secure, introduce reporting verbs for specific moves (argues, reports, proposes, concludes).

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 1,200-word article and twenty minutes to write a 120-word summary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Represents purpose, main argument or findings and conclusion proportionately, uses accurate reporting verbs, and keeps unmarked opinion out.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers the main points but follows paragraph order, over-represents detail or borrows phrasing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises only the introduction, lists details, or misrepresents the main claim.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners summarise textbook sections and short articles. Pre-sessional learners summarise journal articles for extended writing and progression tasks. Taught postgraduates must summarise research articles quickly and accurately for literature reviews and critiques (ges.critique).
reviewNotes: Brown and Day's participants were L1 English-speaking school and college students; their developmental findings are applied to L2 academic summary by analogy.

guidance.summary: Thompson and Ye classified reporting verbs by the kind of act reported and by the evaluation they convey, distinguishing the cited author's stance from the reporting writer's, and Hyland documented disciplinary differences in reporting-verb preferences. Teach verbs in functional groups with their evaluative force, using examples from learners' own disciplines. Emphasise precision over variety: the aim is to represent accurately what the source did and how far the writer accepts it.

activities.title: Stance continuum
learnerActions: Place given reporting verbs on a line from 'writer accepts the claim' to 'writer distances themselves' (demonstrate, show, suggest, claim, allege)
Discuss borderline cases with a partner
Report the same study three times to signal acceptance, neutrality and distance
activities.intendedInsight: Reporting verbs carry the writer's stance towards the reported claim.
activities.rationale: The task draws on Thompson and Ye's distinction between factive, non-factive and counter-factive evaluation.

activities.title: Discipline verb profile
learnerActions: Collect reporting verbs from three articles in your field
Group them by the act reported (research, cognition, discourse)
Compare your profile with a peer from another discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Disciplines prefer different reporting verbs.
activities.rationale: Hyland found clear disciplinary differences in reporting-verb choice; learner-collected data makes these visible in the learner's own field.

difficulties.pattern: I should never repeat a reporting verb.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strained variation that produces inaccurate verbs, such as 'Smith confesses that'
difficulties.response: Explain that accuracy matters more than variety and show expert texts that repeat neutral verbs. Avoid handing out long undifferentiated verb lists.

difficulties.pattern: Claim and state mean the same thing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unintended distancing from, or endorsement of, reported claims
difficulties.response: Contrast verb pairs in context and ask what each implies about the writer's view, linking back to how the source itself commits to its claim.

difficulties.pattern: The author discusses about the problem and emphasises on its causes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Prepositions added to transitive reporting verbs
difficulties.response: Learners often extend the pattern of a related noun ('a discussion about', 'an emphasis on') to the verb. Teach verbs with their complementation from corpus or dictionary examples and practise noun–verb pairs side by side.

diagnostic.task: Give a sentence reporting a study's finding with a blank for the verb, and three contexts: the writer agrees, is neutral, and doubts the finding. Ask for a suitable verb for each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses verbs that convey the intended stance with correct grammar, such as 'demonstrates', 'reports' and 'claims'.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Chooses suitable verbs for two contexts, or makes complementation errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses the same verb throughout, or chooses verbs with unintended stance.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a small set of neutral verbs used accurately. Pre-sessional learners should learn stance contrasts. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates should profile their discipline's verbs, and doctoral researchers need fine control of stance when positioning their own work.

guidance.summary: Swales distinguished integral citations, in which the cited author is part of the sentence, from non-integral ones, and Thompson and Tribble refined these categories using a corpus of theses. Hyland showed that disciplines differ in their balance of forms, with non-integral forms more frequent in the sciences. Teach the forms as rhetorical choices about emphasis, the person or the information, rather than as formatting alternatives.

activities.title: Form spotting and effect
learnerActions: Highlight integral and non-integral citations in two expert paragraphs from different disciplines
Count each type and compare the proportions
Rewrite two citations in the other form and discuss what changed in emphasis
activities.intendedInsight: Citation form changes what the reader notices: the author or the information.
activities.rationale: Comparing disciplines and testing rewrites draws on Hyland's and Thompson and Tribble's analyses of citation form.

activities.title: Revise for emphasis
learnerActions: Revise a paragraph in which every citation is integral
Make established points information-prominent and group supporting sources in a single bracket
Keep author-prominent forms only where a specific scholar's position matters
activities.intendedInsight: Varying citation form helps a paragraph focus on ideas and reserves author prominence for positions.
activities.rationale: Paragraphs built entirely from integral citations tend to read as lists of authors rather than as an account of what is known.

difficulties.pattern: I always start with the author's name; it is clearer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that read 'X (2019) says… Y (2020) says…'
difficulties.response: Show how information-prominent citation foregrounds ideas and supports synthesis. Do not ban integral forms; the aim is choice.

difficulties.pattern: Putting the name in brackets makes the source look less important.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of non-integral forms
difficulties.response: Explain the difference in emphasis and show science writing in which non-integral forms dominate, including for highly cited work.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner one finding supported by three sources and one contested position held by one scholar. Ask for two sentences citing them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses a non-integral citation grouping the three sources for the finding and an integral citation for the contested position, and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses appropriate forms but cannot explain the choice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cites each source separately with integral forms in a list.

guidance.contextNotes: Introduce this on pre-sessional courses once basic in-text citation is secure. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates should analyse the balance of forms in their discipline. Doctoral researchers use citation form strategically in literature reviews and discussion sections.
reviewNotes: The claim that novice paragraphs built from integral citations read as lists of authors is a practitioner observation; no source in the closed bibliography is cited for it.

guidance.summary: Pecorari's linguistic analysis of source use emphasises transparency: readers should be able to tell what comes from a source and what from the writer. Hunston's averral–attribution distinction and Chang and Schleppegrell's work on making stance resources explicit for L2 writers point to teaching the specific language that marks boundaries: continued attribution, citation placement, evaluative commentary and averral markers. The aim is both integrity and a visible authorial voice.

activities.title: Colour the voices
learnerActions: Highlight source content in one colour per source and the writer's own comment in another
Identify sentences that could belong to either
Revise those sentences with attribution or averral markers so that their status is clear
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need linguistic signals to tell source content from the writer's voice.
activities.rationale: Making voices visible applies the averral–attribution distinction and supports transparent source use.

activities.title: Add your voice
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that reports two sources and contains no comment
Add one sentence that evaluates, compares or applies the sources to the paragraph's point
Check with a partner that the new sentence is clearly the writer's
activities.intendedInsight: A paragraph built from sources still needs the writer's own contribution.
activities.rationale: Chang and Schleppegrell argue that L2 writers benefit from explicit teaching of the linguistic resources for taking an authorial stance.

difficulties.pattern: I put one citation at the end of the paragraph to cover everything.
difficulties.revealedBy: Single end-of-paragraph citations covering mixed content
difficulties.response: Show that an end-placed citation leaves the reader unsure what it covers, and teach citation placement and continued attribution.

difficulties.pattern: My own opinion is not allowed in academic writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs consisting entirely of reported content
difficulties.response: Show expert texts in which writers evaluate and connect sources, and distinguish argued evaluation from unsupported personal opinion, without implying the learner's previous context was wrong.

difficulties.pattern: Once I paraphrase it, it becomes my idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrased content presented as the writer's own claim
difficulties.response: Clarify that paraphrase changes the wording, not the ownership of the idea.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to highlight which sentences in a 150-word paragraph from their own draft are attributed and which are their own.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Highlights accurately, and the text itself makes each sentence's status clear to a reader.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Highlights accurately, but some sentences are ambiguous in the text.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish their own claims from source content.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need basic continued attribution. Pre-sessional writing assessment often rewards a visible writer's voice, so make this expectation explicit. For undergraduates and taught postgraduates, boundaries become harder to manage in multi-source paragraphs (see syn.synthesis-paragraphs).

guidance.summary: Style guides permit secondary citation but discourage it where the original can be obtained, because secondary accounts may simplify or distort the original. Teach both the decision and the format: attempt to trace the original through backward chaining, and use secondary citation transparently when the original is unavailable. Learners also need to know which work appears in the reference list in their required style.

activities.title: Trace the classic
learnerActions: Find a classic study reported in a textbook
Try to locate the original from the textbook's reference using the library catalogue
Compare the textbook's account with the original and note any differences
Decide whether to cite the original or use a secondary citation
activities.intendedInsight: Secondary accounts can differ from originals, so tracing the original is worth the effort.
activities.rationale: Comparing accounts shows concretely why style guides prefer citing what was read.

activities.title: Format practice
learnerActions: Write the in-text citation and reference-list entry for a secondary citation in your required style
Check them against the style guide
Explain to a partner which work is listed and why
activities.intendedInsight: Secondary citation has specific format rules that differ between styles.
activities.rationale: Checking against the guide prevents common errors such as listing the unread original.

difficulties.pattern: I list the original because it looks better.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists including works the writer has not read
difficulties.response: Explain that citing and listing the original implies having read it, which misrepresents the writer's research.

difficulties.pattern: Everything I read is in the textbook, so I use 'cited in' for everything.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large numbers of secondary citations in an essay
difficulties.response: Teach backward chaining and set the expectation that key sources are read in the original.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You read about a well-known theory in a textbook by Smith. How do you cite it?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Tries to find the original first; if using Smith, cites the theory as a secondary source and, in APA style, lists only Smith.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Formats correctly but does not mention finding the original.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cites the theorist directly without having read the original.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners who rely on textbooks need this early. Pre-sessional and undergraduate learners should practise chaining to originals. Taught postgraduates should seldom need secondary citation except for unobtainable or inaccessible-language originals.
reviewNotes: Conventions differ between referencing styles; apa2020 is cited for the APA approach only.

guidance.summary: Multilingual learners often have access to relevant scholarship in other languages, and Lillis and Curry show how English-medium publishing privileges some knowledge over other knowledge. Using such sources well requires transparency: translations are marked as the writer's own, the original work is cited, and reference entries follow the style's rules for non-English works. Teach this as a legitimate practice, and encourage learners to check local expectations, since some modules specify English-language sources.

activities.title: Translate and signal
learnerActions: Choose a short passage from a source in another language you read
Write an English quotation of it marked as your own translation, and a separate paraphrase with citation
Write the reference-list entry following your style guide
Ask a peer who shares the language to check the accuracy of the translation
activities.intendedInsight: Non-English sources can be used openly when translation is marked and the original is cited.
activities.rationale: The task practises style-guide conventions and accuracy while treating the plurilingual repertoire as a resource.

activities.title: What does English-only miss?
learnerActions: Discuss whether research on your topic exists in other languages
Consider what perspectives it adds, for example on local contexts
Plan how to raise its use with your tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Non-English scholarship can add perspectives, and its use should be discussed openly.
activities.rationale: Lillis and Curry document inequalities in English-medium publishing; reflecting on them supports informed choices of sources.

difficulties.pattern: I translated it myself, so it is my own writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unmarked translated passages
difficulties.response: Explain that translation changes the language but not the ownership of the ideas; quotation and paraphrase rules still apply.

difficulties.pattern: Machine translation is fine for quotations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inaccurate translated quotations
difficulties.response: Show how to check machine translation against the original and how to declare tool use where policy requires it (see dig.machine-translation). Refer to the local policy rather than banning tools outright.

difficulties.pattern: My tutor will not accept sources in my language.
difficulties.revealedBy: Relevant non-English sources avoided without asking
difficulties.response: Encourage the learner to ask and to explain the source's relevance, presenting their languages as an asset to the work.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show how they would quote and reference a sentence from a source in another language.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Quotes in English marked as their own translation (giving the original if required), cites the original work, and formats the reference with a translated title.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Translates and cites, but does not mark the translation or formats the reference incorrectly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Presents the translated wording as their own without citation.

guidance.contextNotes: This matters wherever learners write about their own contexts, from pre-sessional projects onward. At PGR level, non-English sources may be central to the research, and conventions for presenting originals alongside translations vary by discipline.
reviewNotes: Conventions for presenting original-language text alongside translations vary by discipline and style; local guidance should be checked.

guidance.summary: Spivey describes discourse synthesis as a constructive process in which writers select, organise and connect content from several texts to build a new structure. Feak and Swales show the same contrast at the level of the literature review, where organisation by theme rather than by author is the expected norm. Teaching the concept through contrasting examples (serial summary versus synthesis) gives learners a clear target before they learn the tools and language of synthesis.

activities.title: Two paragraphs, same sources
learnerActions: Read two paragraphs that use the same three sources, one organised source by source and one around a point
Mark the topic sentence and each source's role in both
Discuss which better answers a given question and why
activities.intendedInsight: Synthesis is organised by the writer's idea, not by the sources.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples make the difference between reproducing and transforming source organisation concrete, reflecting Spivey's account of organising and connecting.

activities.title: Find the meeting point
learnerActions: Read three short texts on one topic
Write down one point on which all three can be brought together
Note what each text contributes to that point, including where it differs
activities.intendedInsight: Synthesis starts from a point that connects sources.
activities.rationale: Generating a connecting point is the first constructive move in discourse synthesis.

difficulties.pattern: Synthesis means summarising all the sources in one paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs with several citations that summarise each source in turn
difficulties.response: Use paired examples and ask learners to identify the controlling point; if there is none, the paragraph is a sequence of summaries.

difficulties.pattern: The sources are the experts; who am I to organise them?
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to impose an organising idea on sources
difficulties.response: Present synthesis as interpretive work that experts themselves do in reviews, and model tentative organising claims. Return to the idea that sources serve the writer's purpose.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in their own words and with an example from their reading, the difference between a summary and a synthesis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that synthesis organises several sources around the writer's point and shows how they relate, with a concrete example.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says synthesis uses several sources but does not mention organisation or relationships.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates synthesis with summary or with using many citations.

guidance.contextNotes: Introduce synthesis at foundation level with two or three short texts. Pre-sessional extended writing requires it, and it underpins literature review assignments for undergraduates and taught postgraduates.

guidance.summary: A synthesis matrix externalises the organising and connecting work that Spivey identifies in discourse synthesis: it shows each source's position on each theme and lets learners read across sources. Teacher-set columns provide scaffolding at first; independent generation of columns develops alongside thematic grouping. The matrix is a planning tool rather than an end product, so learners should be shown explicitly how columns become paragraphs.

activities.title: Guided matrix
learnerActions: Receive a matrix with teacher-set columns (for example definition, causes, evidence, limitations)
Fill each cell with brief own-words notes and locators from three sources
Read down each column and write one sentence about agreement or difference
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a matrix by column reveals relationships that reading source by source hides.
activities.rationale: Set columns reduce the organising load so that learners can concentrate on selecting and comparing content.

activities.title: From matrix to plan
learnerActions: Use a completed matrix to choose two columns that answer the question
Turn each column into a paragraph plan with a topic sentence and the sources that support or qualify it
Compare the plan with an author-by-author plan for the same sources
activities.intendedInsight: Matrix columns map onto synthesis paragraphs.
activities.rationale: Making the matrix-to-paragraph link explicit stops the matrix becoming an isolated note-making exercise and reflects the thematic organisation Feak and Swales recommend for reviews.

difficulties.pattern: I copied sentences into the cells to save time.
difficulties.revealedBy: Matrices filled with source wording that later reappears in essays
difficulties.response: Require brief own-words notes in cells, with any copied wording in quotation marks and a locator.

difficulties.pattern: I made the matrix but still wrote about each source in turn.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays organised by matrix row rather than column
difficulties.response: Model writing from a column and have learners plan paragraphs from columns before drafting.

difficulties.pattern: A matrix is too much work for a short essay.
difficulties.revealedBy: Matrices abandoned or not attempted
difficulties.response: Scale the matrix to the task: a three-by-three grid may be enough for a short essay.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to build a matrix from three given abstracts for a given question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses question-relevant columns, writes concise own-words notes and identifies a cross-source pattern.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Builds a matrix with generic columns or copied content.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes a separate summary for each source instead of a grid.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and early pre-sessional stages, provide the columns. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates should generate their own and may use spreadsheets or reference-manager tags. Doctoral researchers often maintain large matrices or literature databases throughout the project.
reviewNotes: No source in the closed bibliography evaluates synthesis matrices directly; the matrix is presented as a practitioner tool consistent with research on discourse synthesis.

guidance.summary: Thematic grouping is the analytical core of literature reviews: Kwan's analysis of doctoral literature reviews found them organised into thematic units, and Feak and Swales present thematic organisation as an alternative to chronological or author-by-author structures. Learners need explicit criteria for grouping (by factor, position, method or finding) and should test alternative groupings before choosing the one that best serves their argument. Classification skills from rhetorical-function work transfer directly.

activities.title: Card sort and re-sort
learnerActions: Write each source's key point on a card
Sort the cards into groups and name each group
Re-sort using a different criterion and decide which grouping better serves the question
activities.intendedInsight: Themes are constructed by the writer, and different groupings suit different arguments.
activities.rationale: Physical sorting makes classification criteria visible and encourages testing alternatives before committing to a structure.

activities.title: Reverse-engineer a review
learnerActions: Read a short published literature review
Identify its themes and the sources under each
Note sources that appear under more than one theme and discuss why
activities.intendedInsight: Expert reviews organise sources by theme, and a source can contribute to several themes.
activities.rationale: Analysing expert reviews reflects genre-analytic studies of the literature review such as Kwan's.

difficulties.pattern: Each source is its own theme.
difficulties.revealedBy: Theme labels that are author names or study titles
difficulties.response: Ask what issue each source addresses, and group by those issues; a matrix with question-based columns can make shared issues visible.

difficulties.pattern: My themes are 'advantages' and 'disadvantages', as in my previous essays.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic template headings unconnected to what the literature discusses
difficulties.response: Show how themes emerge from what sources discuss and relate to the question. Do not reject simple structures where they suit the task; make the classification criterion explicit.

difficulties.pattern: A source can only go in one group.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sources forced into a single group, with relevant content lost
difficulties.response: Show expert reviews in which one study is cited under several themes for different aspects.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner six source summaries and ask for a thematic grouping with a justification.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces coherent, question-related themes, allocates sources (some to several themes) and justifies the criterion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces plausible groups but with vague labels or single-source themes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Groups by author, date or source type only.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, thematic grouping is practised with small source sets for extended essays. Undergraduates need it for literature review assignments. For taught postgraduates and doctoral researchers it organises dissertation and thesis literature reviews (res.literature-review).

guidance.summary: Spivey's connecting operation and Petrić's finding that higher-rated theses used citations for comparison and linking more than lower-rated ones point to the same teaching target: explicit statements of how sources relate. Teach a small set of relationship types (agree, corroborate, extend, qualify, contrast, contradict) with matching language, and require learners to check whether apparent disagreement reflects differences in definition, method or context. This is where reading across texts becomes writing across texts.

activities.title: Relationship labelling
learnerActions: Read pairs of short abstracts
Label each pair's relationship (agree, extend, qualify, contrast, contradict)
Check whether any disagreement is explained by method, sample or definition
Write one sentence expressing each relationship precisely
activities.intendedInsight: Precise relationship labels lead to precise relational language.
activities.rationale: Labelling before writing focuses attention on the connecting operation in discourse synthesis.

activities.title: Upgrade the list
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that cites sources in sequence with 'also' and 'another study'
Rewrite it with explicit relational language and grouped citations
Compare the two versions for what the reader learns
activities.intendedInsight: Explicit relationships turn a list of studies into synthesis.
activities.rationale: Petrić found that higher-rated writing used citations to compare and link, not only to attribute.

difficulties.pattern: Also, another study, furthermore: that shows they are connected.
difficulties.revealedBy: Additive connectors used where the relationship is contrast or qualification
difficulties.response: Require learners to name the relationship before choosing a connector or verb.

difficulties.pattern: The two studies disagree, so one must be wrong.
difficulties.revealedBy: Binary judgements of conflicting findings
difficulties.response: Show how differences in context, sample or measure can explain divergent findings, and practise reading the studies side by side before writing.

difficulties.pattern: I do not know how to say that one study extends another.
difficulties.revealedBy: A narrow range of relational verbs, often only 'says'
difficulties.response: Teach a small set of relational reporting verbs (confirm, extend, challenge, qualify) in context.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner two abstracts with partly conflicting findings and ask for a two-sentence synthesis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the relationship precisely, suggests a reason for the difference and uses accurate relational language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes that the studies differ but does not specify how or why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises each study separately.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners practise with two or three sources. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates need the full range of relationships for essays and reviews; doctoral researchers must represent complex debates fairly and precisely.

guidance.summary: Swales's CARS model identifies counter-claiming, indicating a gap, raising a question and continuing a tradition as ways of establishing a niche, and Kwan found related moves in doctoral literature reviews; Feak and Swales show how reviews build towards such positions. Teach gaps as outcomes of synthesis rather than as formulae: learners should be able to point to the sources and relationships that reveal a gap, and hedge claims about the absence of research in proportion to the search actually done. Identifying significant gaps develops into expert performance, so expectations should rise across stages.

activities.title: Gap with evidence
learnerActions: Use a completed synthesis matrix to find empty cells, conflicting findings and repeated limitations
For each, write a sentence identifying the gap or tension
Annotate each sentence with the matrix evidence that supports it
activities.intendedInsight: Gaps must be grounded in evidence from the literature reviewed.
activities.rationale: Linking each claimed gap to matrix evidence discourages unsupported claims that no research exists.

activities.title: Niche moves in published introductions
learnerActions: Read three research article introductions from your field
Identify how each establishes a niche (gap, counter-claim, question, continuation)
Write a niche statement for your own topic using the most suitable type
activities.intendedInsight: There are several ways to establish a niche, and fields prefer different ones.
activities.rationale: The task applies Swales's analysis of niche establishment, which learners can test against their discipline.

difficulties.pattern: No one has ever studied this.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged absolute gap claims based on a few searches
difficulties.response: Teach hedged formulations and check the claim against a wider map of the field; discuss how expert readers react to overclaiming.

difficulties.pattern: A gap is anything that has not been studied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gaps that are trivial or not worth filling
difficulties.response: Discuss why a gap matters: link it to significance, an unresolved debate or a practical need.

difficulties.pattern: Criticising published research feels disrespectful.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to identify limitations or tensions
difficulties.response: Model respectful critique and show that authors themselves identify limitations; frame gaps as opportunities the field itself recognises.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state a gap in the literature on their topic and show the evidence for it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a specific, hedged gap linked to identified sources and explains why it matters.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a plausible gap but with weak evidence or overclaiming.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify a gap, or claims an absolute gap without evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: Final-year undergraduates need this for dissertations. Taught postgraduates use gaps to justify dissertation questions, and doctoral researchers must articulate gaps that position an original contribution (res.gap-niche).

guidance.summary: Synthesis paragraphs combine argument and source use. Wingate found that students often did not understand that essays require an argument, and Petrić's comparison of high- and low-rated theses suggests that stronger writers use citations to compare and connect rather than only to attribute. Feak and Swales provide models of text that integrates several sources under the writer's point. Teach the paragraph as a sequence of moves: the writer's claim, related sources, commentary, link.

activities.title: Build from a matrix column
learnerActions: Choose a column from a synthesis matrix
Write a topic sentence that states your point about that theme
Add sources grouped by relationship, using non-integral citation for agreement and integral citation for contrasting positions
Add commentary and a closing link to the wider argument
activities.intendedInsight: A synthesis paragraph is built from a theme and a claim, not from a source.
activities.rationale: Moving from matrix to paragraph makes the organising move explicit.

activities.title: Expert paragraph anatomy
learnerActions: Analyse a published synthesis paragraph from your field
Label the writer's claim, each source's role, the relationships and the commentary
Write a parallel paragraph on your own topic using the same structure
activities.intendedInsight: Expert synthesis paragraphs have a recognisable structure that can be adapted.
activities.rationale: Analysis of expert texts followed by parallel writing is a common genre-based approach, and it makes visible the comparing and linking functions Petrić associated with higher-rated writing.

difficulties.pattern: My paragraph starts with the first source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Topic sentences that report a source
difficulties.response: Require a topic sentence in the writer's voice before any sources are added.

difficulties.pattern: With so many sources, I cannot tell where my voice is.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambiguous attribution in multi-source paragraphs
difficulties.response: Teach continued attribution and explicit commentary markers, and colour-code voices in drafts.

difficulties.pattern: Lots of citations in one paragraph shows synthesis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of citations without relationships or commentary
difficulties.response: Ask learners to state what each source contributes and how the sources relate before revising.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 150-word paragraph from a given matrix column.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Opens with the writer's claim, relates sources explicitly, uses appropriate citation forms, comments and links forward.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Integrates sources but lacks commentary, or begins with a source.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Produces a sequence of summaries.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, synthesis paragraphs are a key target for progression writing. Undergraduates and taught postgraduates use them in essays and reviews; doctoral researchers use them throughout the thesis.

guidance.summary: Plakans found that reading-to-write tasks elicited more interactive, recursive composing processes than writing-only tasks, and Plakans and Gebril showed that writers used sources for several purposes, including ideas, organisation and language support. Grabe and Zhang argue that reading and writing should be taught together in EAP, and Hirvela treats reading-to-write connections as central to L2 writing instruction. Teach integrated tasks as a process (task analysis, purposeful reading and listening, selective notes, planning by point, transformation of source language) rather than as test technique, so that it transfers to coursework.

activities.title: Process walkthrough
learnerActions: Analyse an integrated task prompt and underline what must be done with each source
Read and listen with the task in mind, making two-column notes (source point; relevance to the task)
Plan the response by points, then write it within a time limit
Check for copied strings and for explicit relationships between sources
activities.intendedInsight: Integrated tasks reward selection and transformation organised by the task.
activities.rationale: Breaking the process into stages reflects the composing processes observed in reading-to-write tasks and the case for teaching reading and writing together.

activities.title: Source-use audit
